documents.abstract: This study aimed to examine the effect of Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice on student’s speaking skills at SMPN 4 Koto Baru. A quantitative approach with a pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. The participants considered of 27 seventh-grade A student’s selected through total sampling. Data were collected using speaking tests assessing pronunciation, fluency, vocabulary, and grammar. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test. The results showed that the students mean score increased from 34.81 in the pre-test and 44.44 in the post-test. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test yielded a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Therefore, the null hypothesis (H0) was rejected, and the alternative hypothesis (Ha) was accepted. Indicating that Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice has a significant positive effect on students speaking skills. These findings suggest that integrating collaborative learning with AI-assisted speaking practice can serve as an effective strategy for improving students speaking skills.

Abstract The Transport Research and Innovation Monitoring and Information System (TRIMIS) tracks EU-funded transport research and innovation projects to identify trends and inform policymaking. A key function of TRIMIS is maintaining a comprehensive and accurate database of transport projects. Selecting and categorising relevant projects is a manual and time-consuming process. This study explores the use of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically large language models (LLMs), to support and accelerate this task. A workflow was developed using an LLM platform (GENESIS, the JRC internal, secure, general-purpose LLM platform), iteratively refining prompts to match expert human judgment in identifying relevant projects from CORDIS. Comparing LLM-generated outputs to the existing TRIMIS database, projects were assessed for inclusion/exclusion and classified by transport mode and sector, and technology thematic area. The classifications allow for filtering and consequent analysis and visualisation by these categories. A further application investigated was the assessment of projects for their contribution to the competitiveness of the EU Automotive Industry. Prompt engineering iterations and structured output analysis improved accuracy and consistency and reduced the risk of unsupported or fabricated classifications by requiring every positive decision to be grounded in a verbatim quotation from the project text. Using the ensemble configuration, we analysed 52,923 Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe projects (2014–2026), identifying 6,986 relevant for inclusion in the TRIMIS database, with reporting in this paper focused on the most recent 19,025 Horizon Europe projects, of which 2,184 (11.5%) were assessed as relevant. The analysis of the full corpus required about two days of serial model time for the two deployed configurations (Annex 5), reducing manual work and identifying matches in previously overlooked funding sources. Outcomes also helped to re-evaluate existing taxonomies. The results demonstrate the potential of AI-assisted workflows to reduce manual workload, improve accuracy, and scale project curation for the TRIMIS database, with broader implications for using AI-assisted methods in public-sector knowledge management. Future work will explore hybrid human-AI review pipelines and domain-specific fine-tuning.

EPT E INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFIOS E POSSIBILIDADES PARA A FORMAÇÃO DE PROFISSIONAIS NA ERA DIGITAL. VOCATIONAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL EDUCATION AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CHALLENGES AND POSSIBILITIES FOR PROFESSIONAL TRAINING IN THE DIGITAL AGE. EDUCACIÓN PROFESIONAL Y TECNOLÓGICA E INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFÍOS Y POSIBILIDADES PARA LA FORMACIÓN DE PROFESIONALES EN LA ERA DIGITAL. Gabriel Nascimento de Carvalho Simone Helen Drumond Ischkanian Gladys Nogueira Cabral Celine Maria de Sousa Azevedo Silvana Nascimento de Carvalho Sygride Nascimento de Carvalho Sandro Garabed Ischkanian RESUMO A Educação Profissional e Tecnológica (EPT) enfrenta desafios relacionados à incorporação da inteligência artificial nos processos de ensino e aprendizagem, na organização curricular e no desenvolvimento de competências necessárias ao mundo do trabalho. A expansão das tecnologias digitais demanda reflexões sobre as possibilidades de inovação pedagógica, a preparação dos docentes, a formação crítica dos estudantes e as implicações éticas do uso de sistemas inteligentes. Diante desse cenário, estabelece-se como problema de pesquisa: de que maneira a inteligência artificial pode contribuir para a formação de profissionais na EPT, considerando as exigências da transformação digital e os desafios de sua implementação educacional? O objetivo geral consiste em analisar os desafios e as possibilidades da integração da inteligência artificial à formação profissional, com atenção às competências técnicas, digitais, críticas e éticas requeridas na contemporaneidade. Metodologicamente, propõe-se uma pesquisa qualitativa, de caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida por meio de revisão bibliográfica e análise documental de publicações científicas e documentos institucionais pertinentes à temática. A análise permite discutir possibilidades de personalização da aprendizagem, apoio às atividades pedagógicas, simulação de situações profissionais e aproximação entre educação e transformações tecnológicas. Também evidencia desafios relativos à infraestrutura, à formação docente, à proteção de dados, aos vieses algorítmicos e às desigualdades de acesso. Conclui-se que a integração da inteligência artificial à EPT requer planejamento pedagógico, formação continuada e princípios éticos, de modo a articular inovação tecnológica, inclusão educacional e desenvolvimento humano na preparação dos profissionais para a era digital. Palavras-chave: Educação profissional e tecnológica; inteligência artificial; formação profissional; competências digitais. ABSTRACT Professional and Technological Education (PTE) faces challenges related to the incorporation of artificial intelligence into teaching and learning processes, curriculum organization, and the development of skills required in the world of work. The expansion of digital technologies calls for reflection on the possibilities of pedagogical innovation, teacher preparation, students’ critical development, and the ethical implications of using intelligent systems. Against this background, the research problem is formulated as follows: how can artificial intelligence contribute to professional training in PTE, considering the demands of digital transformation and the challenges of its educational implementation? The general objective is to analyze the challenges and possibilities of integrating artificial intelligence into professional education, focusing on the technical, digital, critical, and ethical competencies required in contemporary society. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, based on a literature review and documentary analysis of scientific publications and institutional documents relevant to the topic. The analysis discusses opportunities for personalized learning, support for pedagogical activities, simulation of professional situations, and closer alignment between education and technological change. It also identifies challenges involving infrastructure, teacher training, data protection, algorithmic bias, and unequal access. The study concludes that integrating artificial intelligence into PTE requires pedagogical planning, continuing professional development, and ethical principles to connect technological innovation, educational inclusion, and human development in preparing professionals for the digital age. Keywords: Professional and technological education; artificial intelligence; professional training; digital competencies. El objetivo general consiste en analizar los desafíos y las posibilidades de integrar la inteligencia artificial en la formación profesional, prestando atención a las competencias técnicas, digitales, críticas y éticas requeridas en la sociedad contemporánea. Metodológicamente, se propone una investigación cualitativa, de carácter exploratorio y descriptivo, basada en una revisión bibliográfica y un análisis documental de publicaciones científicas y documentos institucionales pertinentes. Background: Juvenile (adolescent) girls from socio-economically disadvantaged households continue to perform heavy manual material-handling (MMH) tasks in India’s unorganized brick-manufacturing sector, despite legal protections against child labour. Evidence on their ergonomic exposures, physiological strain, and musculoskeletal health remains scarce. Objective: To evaluate the physical workload, postural stress, thermal exposure, musculoskeletal symptom prevalence, and acute physiological responses of juvenile girls employed in manual brick manufacturing units in West Bengal, India. Methods: A cross-sectional study design was adopted involving 100 young females within the age group of 13 to 18 years who worked at brick manufacturing plants in Nadia and Howrah districts of West Bengal. Data collection included interviews using modified Nordic questionnaires, anthropometry, activity observations both direct and video recorded, postural analysis through the Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS), thermal environment assessment, and physiological parameters both pre and post tasks of brick carrying. A paired t-test was performed to assess the physiological parameters before and after brick carrying, while the chi-square test was used to determine any relationship between musculoskeletal symptoms and BMI or the number of bricks handled per day. Results: The mean age was 15.5±2.33 years, BMI was 18.90±1.52 kg/m² and the occupational experience was 1.3±0.6 years. In general, 91% of participants complained of job-related pain, including the head (72%), neck (72%), and leg (78%). Neck pain was statistically correlated with chronic energy deficiencies (BMI < 18.5 kg/m², χ² = 9.675, p = 0.0019). Lifting more than 2,000 bricks per day was statistically correlated with head pain (χ² = 6.722, p = 0.0095), neck pain (χ² = 4.228, p = 0.0397), shoulder pain (χ² = 4.396, p = 0.0360), and back pain (χ² = 10.306, p = 0.0013). Bricks lifting led to a significant increase in heart rate (from 80.33±3.67 to 112.45±2.13 beats/min, p < 0.05), systolic blood pressure (from 119.7±3.5 to 134.9±5.15 mmHg, p < 0.05), and perceived exertion level (from 13.2±1.5 to 18.6±0.45). Participants performed 45% of the tasks moderately and 25% heavily; unloading bricks from the kiln top was the most dangerous according to the OWAS scale. Conclusion: Manual brick production entails heavy postural, thermal, and cardiovascular stress along with extremely high levels of musculoskeletal symptoms in female juveniles. There is an urgent need for intervention measures regarding ergonomics, nutrition, regulation, and education, including the abolition of hazardous juvenile labor, mechanization of load carrying, load restriction, rest breaks, hydration, safe postures, and schooling.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine educators’ perceptions of the ethical boundaries for using artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and academic assessment, distinguishing AI support from AI delegation using flipped learning as a pedagogical lens. Design/methodology/approach A questionnaire was administered to 148 faculty members from Universidade Autónoma de Lisboa, Portugal. The paper adopts an exploratory quantitative case-study design. Analysis used descriptive statistics, normalized Shannon entropy, Pearson correlation and a paired-samples t-test. Findings Respondents were open to AI support for routine, preparatory and lower-order learning activities, but more cautious when AI was associated with evaluation, fairness, interpretation and assessment decisions. Teacher judgment was strongly prioritized, while trust in AI-generated fair and unbiased evaluation remained limited. Entropy analysis showed relatively clear boundaries around AI bias and human judgment, but more contested boundaries around AI-supported evaluation, learner independence and critical reflection. Research limitations/implications The single-institution convenience sample should be interpreted as exploratory and analytically transferable rather than statistically generalizable. Practical implications Institutions should clarify where AI may support assessment and where human evaluative authority must remain explicit. Social implications The findings highlight the need for shared institutional norms. Originality/value The paper proposes the dual approach as an interpretive framework connecting ethical responsibility, cognitive complexity and flipped learning to distinguish AI support from delegated evaluative authority. Its contribution lies in locating the ethical boundary at the transfer of assessment responsibility and identifying where educators’ perceptions indicate crisp or fuzzy boundaries.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: It is assumed that the synergies created by the 6G communication technologies, blockchain organizations, and smart healthcare systems will introduce Society 5.0 in the form of the hyper-connected and patient-centric secure health ecosystem. These technologies are expected to provide an opportunity of unprecedented socio-economic value by real-time remote health monitoring and interaction, decentralized patient data management systems, and clinical decision making based on artificial intelligence. It is not only an ethical and societal but also a legal and regulatory challenge. Patient privacy, ownership of data, bias in the algorithm, and cyber security will have to be taken into consideration before we go into full deployment. Also, there exists no unified legal framework, as well as there are cross-border regulations to back a blockchain empowered contributor-led 6G healthcare system. The chapter will discuss ethical implications, legal issues, and regulations involved with 6G and blockchain-enabled health care and answer the question of what patients should think about informed consent when offered AI-led care, liability when making independent choices, and what the compliance with the right of the citizens to privacy under the jurisdiction of their nation (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), and what regulatory models might be available to decentralized health systems. We finally make high level recommendation concerning future policies and regulation to strike a balance between innovation, patient safety and social trust by the people.

Large language models (LLMs) have been investigated for clinical documentation, with concerns about hallucinations and factual errors. Clinician review and revision of LLM-generated drafts are considered essential; however, the impact of such a workflow on both documentation time and quality remains unknown. This single-center, parallel-group, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) pilot trial evaluated whether a clinician-in-the-loop workflow improves clinical documentation time and quality compared with clinician-only drafting. From February 18 to March 14, 2025, at the Department of Ophthalmology, Kyoto University Hospital, 21 physicians were randomized, and 17 completed the intervention. Participants were randomized to either the Clinician-in-the-loop group or the Clinician-only group. Participants created discharge summaries and referrals for six simulated patient records. The Clinician-in-the-loop group reviewed and edited LLM-generated drafts, whereas the Clinician-only group drafted documents from scratch using matched templates. Unedited LLM drafts formed the LLM-only group. Seventeen physicians submitted 48 discharge summaries and 48 discharge referrals in the Clinician-in-the-loop group, 54 of each document type in the Clinician-only group, and 48 of each in the LLM-only group. Clinician-in-the-loop showed a shorter creation time for summaries (β = −59.4 seconds; 95% CI, −150.6 to 31.7; P = .18) and a longer creation time for referrals (β = 52.9 seconds; 95% CI, −7.0 to 112.9; P = .08) than Clinician-only, although neither difference was statistically significant. In most expert-rated quality domains, the clinician-in-the-loop workflow outperformed clinician-only drafting. LLM-only drafts were fastest but had the lowest quality. In conclusion, a clinician-in-the-loop approach generally improved document quality and, although the primary analysis showed no statistically significant difference in documentation time, suggested potential time savings for certain document types. These findings highlight the importance of active clinician supervision and support further evaluation of clinician-in-the-loop workflows in real-world clinical settings. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT07187050 (registered on September 18, 2025).

documents.abstract: A prevailing belief in quantitative finance is that deploying high-capacity foundation models inevitably generates superior predictive edge (Gu, Kelly, & Xiu, 2020). This paper presents an empirical evaluation testing whether zero-shot foundation forecasting (Google TimesFM 1.0-200M; Das, Kong, Sen, & Zhou, 2024) and kinematic derivatives physics enhance strike selection and compounding in systematic options selling across Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG), and NVIDIA (NVDA) over a continuous 10-year cycle (October 2016 to October 2026 | 2,512 trading days), strictly partitioned into a 5-year In-Sample calibration epoch and a 5-year Out-of-Sample holdout period. We simulate mechanical options compounding under an idealized Zero-VRP invariant (pricing all contracts at zero implied-volatility premium via analytical Black-Scholes-Merton) to isolate pure directional and timing alpha from structural volatility premium capture. On this invariant benchmark, baseline rule-based mechanics achieve terminal equity of $2,349,600 on AMZN (23.50x), $821,300 on GOOG (8.21x), and $27,998,700 on NVDA (280.0x). Integrating TimesFM 10-day ahead forecasts to write defensive call overlays produces zero statistically detectable forecast edge: directional accuracy is indistinguishable from coin flips (50.8% AMZN, 51.2% GOOG, 49.8% NVDA; Diebold-Mariano p-values 0.27, 0.11, 0.42), while call truncation inflicts catastrophic opportunity cost on explosive trend legs (NVDA terminal wealth collapses from 280.0x to 10.9x). Furthermore, kinematic dip-buying rules (velocity-acceleration phase triggers) display severe parameter decay out of sample: on AMZN, out-of-sample terminal wealth sits at the 72.4th percentile of an uninformed random-put placebo (p = 0.28). Deflated Sharpe Ratios (DSR; Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 2014) across all evaluated machine learning enhancements fall to 0.00, demonstrating that the observed historical outperformance was a product of selection bias across non-stationary market regimes.

This study aims to evaluate the implementation of digital Arabic language learning among students enrolled in an Arabic Language Education Study Program at a state university in Makassar, Indonesia, using the Context, Input, Process, and Product (CIPP) evaluation model. This study employed a qualitative evaluative approach, with the head of the study program, lecturers, and students participating as research participants. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the interactive model developed by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, comprising data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that, in the context dimension, the implementation of digital Arabic language learning aligns with the needs of digital transformation and the demands of twenty-first-century education. In the input dimension, digital infrastructure, institutional support, and lecturers’ competencies were generally adequate, although variations in students’ digital literacy remained evident. In the process dimension, digital learning facilitated student interaction, participation, and flexibility in learning. In the product dimension, the implementation contributed to improvements in Arabic language proficiency, learner autonomy, and students’ digital literacy. Overall, the findings indicate that the implementation of digital Arabic language learning was generally effective and warrants further development. This study recommends strengthening technological infrastructure, providing continuous digital literacy training, and optimizing the integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into Arabic language learning.

Abstract Mechanistic models, expressed as simulations that can be run and visualised, are a powerful way to understand biological and other systems. Building them, however, requires formulating mathematical or rule‐based descriptions and translating them into working code, skills that many ecologists and other disciplinary researchers do not have. Generative AI can now perform much of this translation, making mechanistic modelling accessible to researchers, educators and students previously excluded by its technical demands. But delegating this translation to AI also carries real risks: modelling assumptions can become hidden, plausible but incorrect code can pass unnoticed, and the skills and critical habits that model building once developed may never form. We examine the benefits and risks of using generative AI as a modelling companion at each stage of model development (conceptual specification, formalisation, implementation and exploration), drawing on recent experimental evidence on AI‐assisted learning and on a worked predator–prey example built with AI, with a rule‐based epidemic model as a parallel case. At each stage we identify where consequential decisions are silently delegated to the AI and set out practical mitigations that keep human judgement engaged without requiring the technical skills AI has made optional: specifying the conceptual model explicitly before engaging AI, having the AI translate its formalisation back into plain language, testing the implementation against outcomes known from domain knowledge and designing the interface to support interrogation. This new opportunity is substantial: researchers, educators and students who understand their systems but have never been able to build models of them are now able to explore these systems mechanistically, testing how components interact and how the system responds to conditions it has not yet experienced, questions that correlative approaches alone cannot answer. Used carelessly, AI risks eroding modelling skill for little lasting benefit, but used deliberately, in the ways set out here, it opens a new pathway to mechanistic understanding without removing the critical thinking the old technical barrier once enforced.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming public health decision-making, shifting it from descriptive epidemiological reporting to predictive, accelerated operational guidance. Yet AI in public health is discussed almost entirely at technical or regulatory levels, leaving a gap in executive-level guidance. Public health operates within a complex landscape of social determinants, political scrutiny, and incomplete information, where algorithmic errors can severely damage public trust. Consequently, executive competency must expand beyond traditional data interpretation to foundational AI literacy. Leaders must differentiate among diverse AI applications and evaluate their risk profiles, including balancing AI trained on individual-level precision medicine models with public health population-level prevention mandate. Continuous human oversight and multidisciplinary validation should be standard for modern public health organizations. Automated systems must equitably advance population health outcomes under final human authority at all times. Public health executives can better prepare to make informed decisions about AI-related risks using the decision points presented in this commentary.

documents.abstract: In this study, three software reliability tasks are considered: predicting defect prone modules, software incidents severity classification, and predicting deployment change failures, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is studied for those tasks. For four explicitly synthetic tabular datasets with 2,400 data points each, that is, 7,200 observations, four classifiers were tested: logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomized trees and histogram gradient boosting. We were able to generate 12 model task evaluations, with 600 instances left out for each task. The accuracy and the macro-F1 scores of logistic regression were 77.17% and 75.40% for defect prediction, 72.00% and 72.33% for incident severity classification, and 64.33% and 63.69% for change-failure prediction, respectively. There are three areas of examination in the evaluation: predictive performance analysis, error patterns analysis, and model interpretation analysis. The confusion matrix, the receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and the balanced accuracy are all used to explore these areas, along with the Matthews correlation coefficient and the feature-importance analysis. Twenty publications on the topic are critically examined and used to put the benchmark into the context and its methodological choices. The study offers an evaluation protocol that conveys the explanation in terms that the reader can follow and a comparative simulation framework of three software engineering decision points, along with a discussion of the constraints of the shown tasks when it comes to deployment. It does not develop a new learning algorithm but rather it is methodological and comparative. The results reported here are only applicable to the data sets generated and external validity has not been established. Conclusions regarding the practical effectiveness and suitability to deployment of the operational software data should be based on an independent evaluation prior to their use.

documents.abstract: This study aims to investigate scholars’ and researchers’ perceptions, attitudes, and intentions toward using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic research. Employing a cross-sectional survey, data were collected from 1,283 participants in China. After removing missing values, 1150 valid responses were analyzed. Results indicate that perceived usefulness of GenAI was positively associated with attitudes (β = 0.489, p < 0.001) and directly associated with usage intention (β = 0.385, p < 0.001). Furthermore, attitudes toward GenAI had a positive effect on usage intention (β = 0.323, p < 0.001) and mediated the association between perceived usefulness and intention (indirect effect = 0.157, Boot95% CI [0.120, 0.199]). These findings underscore that positive perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness are associated with more favorable attitudes and stronger intentions to adopt it in research. By applying the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to GenAI adoption, this study highlights the need for academic institutions to promote responsible use through ethical guidelines, training programs, and awareness campaigns, which may facilitate effective integration into research practices.

Abstract Objective: Chagas disease remains an important public health problem, particularly in Latin America, where chronic infection frequently leads to cardiac involvement and associated structural changes. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have enabled automated image analysis of chest X-ray (CXR) in several clinical applications, yet little is known about its applicability to Chagas disease. However, the potential of these methods for Chagas disease screening remains largely unexplored. Approach: In this study, we investigate the feasibility of DL models to identify patients with Chagas disease from CXR images. A private dataset of CXRs was used to train and evaluate several convolutional neural network architectures. Main results: Among the evaluated models, EfficientNet-B4 achieved the best overall performance metrics, with accuracy of 0.655 ± 0.026, precision of 0.653 ± 0.041, recall of 0.700 ± 0.157, F1-score of 0.664 ± 0.076, and AUC of 0.727 ± 0.015. Significance: These results indicate that CXRs contain subtle imaging features associated with chronic Chagas disease that can be partially captured by DL models, although the overall discriminative performance remains moderate. While CXR-based DL models are unlikely to serve as a standalone diagnostic tool, they may have potential as complementary screening or triage tools, particularly in settings where chest radiographs are routinely acquired and access to specialized diagnostic testing is limited.. These findings highlight both the feasibility and the limitations of applying artificial intelligence to support Chagas disease screening using routinely acquired radiographic images.

documents.abstract: Background Intelligent automation has gained relevance in business management because of its ability to optimize processes, improve information, and support decision-making. However, there is limited evidence on the organizational conditions that may modify its relationship with financial decisions in Peruvian MSEs. Methods A quantitative, applied, non-experimental, and cross-sectional study was conducted with 372 managers of service MSEs in Chiclayo, selected through simple random sampling. A 36-item questionnaire with a five-category Likert scale was administered, and descriptive analyses, Spearman correlations, and moderated regression with centered variables and HC3 robust errors were used, complemented by slopes and the Johnson-Neyman procedure. Results Intelligent automation was positively and significantly associated with financial decisions (B = .404; p < .001) and explained 28.5% of their variability. The global interactions with digitalization and managerial experience were not individually significant, although their joint evaluation was significant (p = .045). In the dimensional model, only the interaction trust in results × digitalization was significant (B = .120; p = .009). Conclusions Intelligent automation was favorably related to financial decisions, especially in firms with higher levels of digitalization.

documents.abstract: Expert advice on crop management is often written informally, and in such text a number can easily be assigned the wrong role or attached to the wrong operation, material, or measurement basis. We propose QS-IE, a knowledge extraction method constrained by quantity and operation scope. Its unit of extraction is a complete quantitative fact. Given a shared set of numeric candidates and a single base model, QS-IE selects complete candidates from several prompting strategies, verifies them against the source text, and applies scope constraints, so that every extracted quantity stays linked to its source evidence. We built a corpus of 4006 texts on tomato cultivation. Two researchers with agronomy backgrounds jointly annotated and reviewed 1000 of them; the other 3006 were annotated with large language model assistance and then reviewed by hand. The corpus was split into 3206 development texts and 800 independent test texts. On the 1152 reference facts of the test set, QS-IE reached a precision of 84.02%, a recall of 86.72%, and a micro-averaged F1 of 85.35%, which is 3.91 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, a multi-strategy in-context learning ensemble. Removing the operation scope constraints lowered test F1 by 8.24 percentage points. In a sampled human audit of the test set, 82.00% of the outputs for texts containing target facts were judged usable, and all six engineering checks on storage and evidence traceability were passed. The results indicate that explicit association constraints make quantitative facts extracted from tomato cultivation texts more complete and easier to review, which supports the structured, traceable storage of experiential knowledge that experts express in non-standardized text.

Abstract Extrusion technology has emerged as one of the most versatile processing methods for developing functional foods from Andean grains, responding to the increasing global demand for nutritious, sustainable, and gluten-free products. This review critically examines recent advances in the extrusion processing of quinoa, kiwicha, and kañiwa, with emphasis on the interactions between raw material composition, thermomechanical processing parameters, and final product functionality. The review discusses the influence of formulation strategies, extrusion conditions, and specific mechanical energy on starch gelatinisation, protein texturisation, expansion behaviour, and bioactive compound retention. Furthermore, it evaluates the application of conventional and emerging approaches, including high-moisture extrusion, artificial intelligence-based process optimisation, machine learning, and Industry 4.0 technologies, to improve process control and product quality. Current evidence demonstrates that the synergistic integration of ingredient design, extrusion engineering, and predictive modelling is essential for maximising nutritional value, technological performance, and industrial scalability. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on extrusion conditions or grain composition independently, this study presents an integrated techno-functional framework linking formulation strategies, extrusion parameters, nutritional outcomes, and industrial applications. This framework identifies key interactions and research gaps to support the rational design of next-generation extruded foods with enhanced functionality, improved nutritional quality, and sustainable commercial competitiveness.

documents.abstract: This study explores how undergraduate Generation Z students at an international college in Thailand adopt and use AI chatbots. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a sensitizing framework, we conducted an exploratory convergent mixed-methods survey of 144 eligible students. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics and exploratory factor analysis of seven adoption items adapted from TAM and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), while qualitative analysis used LLM-assisted, researcher-verified coding of 127 and 117 substantive open-ended responses to examine motivations and desired features. The analysis suggested two provisional adoption-related dimensions, perceived relational value and social endorsement, and practical accessibility, although the factor-retention criteria were divided between one and two factors. Almost all students selected academic assistance as a reason for using AI chatbots (92.4%). Asked specifically about AI companions, students most often cited information seeking and convenience (27.6% of substantive responses), while personal and emotional support and reservations about companion use were raised in 20.5% and 19.7% of responses, respectively. Human-like interaction was the most frequently requested feature category (39.3%), followed by technical capabilities and academic tools such as citation support. The study contributes exploratory, cross-sectional evidence on AI chatbot adoption in a Thai higher-education context and highlights the importance of balancing practical utility, relational expectations, and clear human-AI boundaries.

ABSTRACT The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into academic writing has raised ethical questions about intellectual property, authorship, and knowledge representation. Although existing research has examined academic integrity and AI literacy, how learners negotiate responsibility when responding to biased or culturally inappropriate AI‐generated outputs remains underexplored. Grounded in critical applied linguistics and informed by relational accountability and distributed agency, this study examines how students enacted accountability in an AI bias analysis task within an undergraduate English academic writing course at a Chinese university. Drawing on group reports, AI interaction records, reflective writing, field notes, and interviews, thematic analysis identified three interrelated orientations through which students enacted accountability: epistemic accountability (evaluating knowledge claims), relational accountability (negotiating responsibility across human‐AI relations), and ecological accountability (questioning the broader linguistic, cultural, and epistemic consequences of AI‐generated knowledge). These orientations reveal accountability as distributed across epistemic judgments, social and technological relations, and broader conditions of knowledge representation. We conceptualize this configuration as distributed accountability: a situated process through which learners negotiate and enact answerability for AI‐mediated knowledge and its consequences. By demonstrating this expansion of answerability, the study connects the micro‐ethics of classroom practice with the macro‐ethics of linguistic and epistemic diversity and equity in AI‐mediated knowledge production. It offers implications for future research on academic writing ethics, critical AI literacy, and educational AI governance in applied linguistics.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Faculty development programmes must adapt to changing expectations in curriculum design, assessment, educational scholarship, technology, leadership and interprofessional practice. The Diploma in Medical Education (Dip. Med. Ed.) at the Defence Services Medical Academy (DSMA), Myanmar, provides a longitudinal example of such adaptation. In 2024, DSMA and the Military Institute of Nursing and Paramedical Sciences (MINP) combined their contributions to the programme, marking a new collaborative phase in its development. This study examined how the DSMA Dip. Med. Ed. programme changed between 2010 and 2026 and to identify the principal curricular and institutional transitions that moved it from foundational faculty development toward contemporary health professions education, including the development of DSMA-MINP collaboration from 2024. We conducted a retrospective documentary analysis using course handbooks from the first course in 2010-2011 through the 16th course handbook in 2026. A structured extraction framework examined programme aims, duration, curriculum architecture, teaching-learning strategies, educational technology, assessment, leadership, communication and professionalism, educational research, workshops and governance. The authors compared documents chronologically and synthesized recurring patterns and material changes into developmental phases. Five phases were identified: foundation and formalisation (2010-2013); consolidation of the modular faculty-development model (2014-2019); outcomes, constructive alignment and digitally supported delivery (2020-2023); DSMA-MINP collaboration and curricular expansion (2024-2025); and further curriculum modernisation (2026). The 2026 curriculum incorporated outcome-based and competency-based medical education, curriculum mapping, quality assurance and accreditation, interprofessional education, problem- and case-based learning, e-learning, simulation, artificial intelligence and AI ethics, educational governance, professionalism, research ethics and critical appraisal. The Dip. Med. Ed. retained a stable core mission while progressively broadening from teacher preparation to a more integrated health professions education programme. The combination of DSMA and MINP from 2024 and the subsequent curricular developments through 2026 represent important milestones in this transformation. Future evaluation should determine whether these intended curriculum changes translate into sustained changes in educational practice, scholarship and institutional outcomes.

The development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications has profound implications for higher education,including student behaviors, engagement, and productivity in learning. While academic literature addressing the implications of AI applications is on the rise, its relevance for fields of economics, business,and the social sciences remains disparate and localized. In this regard, this paper analyzes the bibliometric landscape of AI research using a set of indicators that include keyword co-occurrence, time and research density, and emerging research fronts using VOSviewer, and the search was limited to Scopus-indexed journal articles (2000-2025).A descriptive analysis was done based on three sets of documents, namely the global baseline, the discipline-specific body of work,and a local Malaysian dataset. The global dataset has produced a mature and integrated network with a primary emphasis on educational data mining and learning analytics.Nevertheless, temporal overlay visualization analysis reveals a sharp transition to the human and ethical factors surrounding generative artificial intelligence, including academic integrity and frameworks for evaluating teacher acceptance of disruptive technologies. In contrast, the Malaysian dataset was found to have a sparsely connected network, suggesting the growing nature of local research. Indeed, studies pertaining to Malaysia appear to focus on the interactions between students and ChatGPT and lack psychological theories in any of the included works.This study has identified the fundamental disconnect between regional and international research practices.As such, it can serve as the foundation for future studies that seek to understand the effects of artificial intelligence on the emotional,social, and academic development of students in developed digital economies.

Many enterprise generative AI initiatives stall between a successful pilot and dependable production use. Industry forecasts suggest that at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept, and that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. This paper argues that the gap is primarily a management and delivery problem rather than a model-capability problem, and proposes a practitioner framework for go-live decisions. The framework rests on a single organizing analogy, treating an AI system like a new hire, and translates it into seven readiness checks (value, ownership, data, evaluation, guardrails, operations and adoption), six hard stops that block launch regardless of overall score, an eight-part evidence pack, a 0–2 scoring rubric, and an additional control set for agentic systems that can take actions. The checks are mapped to established sources including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and empirical work on machine learning engineering. Seven publicly documented cases are used to illustrate the failure modes each check is designed to catch. The paper closes with limitations and a proposed agenda for empirical validation. JEL classification: M15, O32, O33.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping graduate employability by changing how competencies are enacted, valued, and developed. While traditional employability frameworks identify competencies expected of graduates, limited research has examined how these competencies may be evolving within AI-enabled environments. This study examines established employability competency domains and explores faculty perceptions of emerging capability requirements in the age of generative AI. A sequential mixed-method design was adopted. Quantitative data from 177 graduating business students in Saudi Arabia were analysed using domain-level principal component analysis to assess the internal structure and reliability of seven established competency domains. Semi-structured interviews with twelve business faculty members were subsequently analysed thematically. The quantitative findings provide context-specific support for communication, leadership, critical thinking and problem-solving, teamwork, management capability, ICT capability, and professionalism. The qualitative findings identified three complementary patterns of perceived competency evolution: human-centric enduring competencies, AI-augmented competencies, and emerging AI-specific competencies. The findings suggest that AI-ready employability involves both the continuing relevance of established competencies and changes in how competencies are enacted alongside intelligent technologies. The study proposes an exploratory AI-ready employability framework integrating established competencies with perceived competency continuity, augmentation, and emergence, providing a foundation for further empirical investigation and curriculum development in AI-integrated higher education.

In light of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are drastically altering creative environments, this chapter addresses Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration Models. LLMs provide previously unheard-of skills in data analysis, content creation with sophisticated reasoning, their successful application requires a sophisticated awareness of their drawbacks, such as their vulnerability to bias, factual inaccuracies, and a lack of practical experience. In order to bridge this gap, hybrid models create organized frameworks that integrate the unique advantages of artificial and human intelligence in a complementary way. In this chapter different collaborative architectures, with an emphasis on models that range from AI-driven workflows with human oversight (where LLM directs the process and a human provides crucial validation and ethical correction) to AI augmentation (where the human is the primary decision-maker and LLM serves as an assistant). The ‘human-in-the-loop’ mechanism is essential to these models because it ensures accountability, quality control, and the application of ethical judgment and contextual knowledge—all of which are now outside the purview of even the most sophisticated LLMs. Through case studies that highlight best practices for task decomposition, interaction design, and performance measurements, the chapter explores the real-world applications of these concepts in domains such as technical writing, software development, and strategic decision-making. At last, hybrid models are needed to minimize LLM risks and for enabling new steps of creativity and productivity, deciding the movement of human-computer interaction in the generative AI.

Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education (HE) worldwide, yet evidence from Asia remains limited. This study examines how students, teachers, and other stakeholders in Asia perceive the role of GenAI in HE, identifying current usage trends and analysing how GenAI is incorporated into academic and pedagogical practices. Using a mixed methods design, the study gathered quantitative data through online surveys of undergraduate students and teachers. Qualitative insights were obtained through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews with a sample of participants, including policymakers, educationists, I/NGO representatives, and IT sector professionals. Findings show that the research participants hold mixed views about the role of GenAI in HE, with some indications of integration into academic practices. The study provides insights into emerging GenAI practices in Asian HE and highlights implications for policy and pedagogical development.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in learning enables students to delegate some cognitive processes to technology, a practice known as cognitive offloading. Although this practice may improve efficiency, using AI without critical evaluation may contribute to an illusion of competence, defined as a discrepancy between perceived understanding and actual performance. This study examined the relationship between AI-based cognitive offloading and the illusion of competence, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking among high school students in Makassar. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design and purposive sampling were employed, involving 356 students aged 15–18 years. Cognitive offloading was measured using an adapted Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking using the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, and the illusion of competence through the discrepancy between Judgment of Learning and performance on an objective PISA-based test. Data were analyzed using Confirmatory Factor Analysis and path analysis in Mplus 8.4. The CFA results indicated acceptable measurement models for cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Path analysis showed that cognitive offloading was positively associated with the illusion of competence and negatively associated with critical thinking, while critical thinking was negatively associated with the illusion of competence. The significant indirect effect indicated complementary partial mediation. These findings highlight the importance of analyzing, evaluating, and verifying AI-generated output to support accurate judgments of understanding. ABSTRAK Penggunaan artificial intelligence (AI) generatif dalam pembelajaran memungkinkan pelajar menyerahkan sebagian proses kognitif kepada teknologi atau melakukan cognitive offloading. Meskipun meningkatkan efisiensi, penggunaan tanpa evaluasi kritis dapat menimbulkan illusion of competence, yaitu ketidaksesuaian antara keyakinan terhadap pemahaman dan performa aktual. Penelitian ini bertujuan menguji hubungan cognitive offloading berbasis AI dengan illusion of competence serta peran mediasi critical thinking pada pelajar SMA di Kota Makassar. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain cross-sectional correlational dan purposive sampling, melibatkan 356 pelajar berusia 15–18 tahun. Cognitive offloading diukur menggunakan adaptasi Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking menggunakan Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, sedangkan illusion of competence dioperasionalkan melalui ketidaksesuaian antara Judgment of Learning dan tes objektif berbasis PISA. Data dianalisis menggunakan Confirmatory Factor Analysis dan path analysis pada Mplus 8.4. Hasil CFA menunjukkan bahwa model pengukuran cognitive offloading dan critical thinking memiliki kesesuaian yang dapat diterima. Path analysis menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading berhubungan positif dengan illusion of competence dan negatif dengan critical thinking, sedangkan critical thinking berhubungan negatif dengan illusion of competence. Efek tidak langsung melalui critical thinking juga signifikan dan menunjukkan complementary partial mediation. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa kemampuan menganalisis, mengevaluasi, dan memverifikasi keluaran AI merupakan bagian penting dalam menjaga ketepatan pelajar ketika menilai pemahamannya.

Generative AI has made plausible output abundant and cheap, but plausibility is not evidence and evidence is not authority. Leading AI assistants already concede this in the notice beneath every prompt box, telling users the system can make mistakes and asking them to check — handing the work of verification to individuals without instruments, records or authority. This working paper proposes Computational Trust Engineering (CTE), an engineering discipline for the path from a language model’s completion to an organization’s consequence. It separates three selections that current practice collapses into one: a generative selection (which continuation is probable?), an evidentiary selection (which candidate is supportable?) and an authority selection (may the supported candidate produce consequence?). CTE grounds these in four realities (human, AI, actual and governance reality) and treats familiar failure modes as measurable gaps between them. It frames evidentiary selection as metrology, with the individual claim as the counted unit, “unknown” as a legitimate result, calibrated instruments and traceable provenance. It introduces attention as the allocation of scarce measurement effort, and states when a language model may serve as an instrument. The paper defends the three-layer separation through collapse analysis and precedent from internal control, functional safety and metrology. It also maps CTE to the NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42001, assurance cases and the EU AI Act, and closes with deployment postures, five falsifiable hypotheses and a research agenda.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI has influenced research on AI literacy education at the elementary school level. A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted to study implementations of Generative AI and methods of AI literacy education in elementary education. The review data includes 211 studies published from 2021 to January 2026 identified from SCOPUS, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Taylor & Francis. Thematic content analysis was used to identify and analyze themes in the review data to examine how the research field has developed after the release of Generative AI technology. The analysis identifies fundamental issues affecting the implementation of Generative AI in elementary education, including concerns about human interaction, varying approaches to ethical questions, and frequent concerns regarding the reliability of Generative AI outputs. The definition of the ethical dimensions of critical AI literacy is found to be inconclusive, calling for a broader adoption of critical AI literacy education at the elementary school level. Established use cases of Generative AI are identified, especially with self-regulated learning and foreign language studies. A holistic and integrated approach to AI literacy education for students and pre-service teachers is supported by the analysis. This study identifies research gaps for longitudinal research on Generative AI in elementary schools, parents’ role in students’ AI literacy, and a need to reach a scholarly consensus on the definition of AI ethics.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely expected to transform professional practices across multiple sectors, including the legal profession. This article critically examines the growing integration of GenAI tools into legal work and the implications this development carries for professional competence, ethical responsibility, and the broader institutional structure of legal practice. While AI promises substantial gains in efficiency by automating tasks such as legal research, document drafting, information retrieval, and data analysis, their adoption also raises significant concerns regarding reliability, transparency, confidentiality, and professional accountability. While prevailing narratives surrounding AI adoption in law often frame technological integration as both inevitable and normatively desirable, emphasising efficiency and competitive advantage while downplaying potential risks and value conflicts, the increasing delegation of professional tasks to algorithmic systems challenges traditional understandings of legal expertise, particularly in relation to judgement, reasoning, and professional autonomy. Moreover, unequal access to advanced AI tools and proprietary datasets may reinforce structural inequalities within the legal market, benefitting larger firms while disadvantaging smaller practices. This article argues for a balanced approach that combines technological literacy with strong ethical frameworks and institutional safeguards. Ultimately, responsible integration of GenAI requires sustained human oversight and collective professional engagement to ensure that technological innovation supports, rather than undermines, the core values of legal practice.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how knowledge-oriented generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool use (GAIU) is associated with sports communication knowledge creation intention (SCKCI), with digital literacy (DL) and individual absorptive capacity (IAC) as sequential capability pathways. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 616 university students in Yunnan Province, China, with sport-related academic backgrounds or sports communication experience was analysed using confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable structural equation modelling and 5,000 resample bootstrap mediation. Composite-score mediation served as a robustness check. Findings Both specific indirect paths and the sequential GAIU–DL–IAC–SCKCI path were significant, while the direct association remained significant, yielding a pattern consistent with partial sequential mediation. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, self-reported and region-specific design does not establish causal or temporal ordering and limits generalisability. SCKCI reflects intention rather than observed behaviour. Practical implications GenAI-supported knowledge work should incorporate source verification, human review and traceability. Social implications Responsible GenAI use in public-facing sports communication requires attention to misinformation, accountability and public trust. Originality/value This study conceptualises GenAI-mediated external knowledge input as generative yet epistemically uncertain and advances a verification-before-absorption logic that distinguishes the epistemic qualification of AI-generated information from its subsequent assimilation and transformation.

This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper presents a generative AI-driven framework designed for e-commerce brand marketing, which integrates marketing content generation with user response prediction. By combining product information, brand characteristics, user behavior data, and contextual information, the framework generates semantically aligned marketing content and predicts user responses, such as click-through rates and purchase intentions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several baseline models in content generation and user response prediction tasks. The framework provides practical support for personalized marketing, content delivery, and decision-making. Moreover, it exhibits strong robustness under challenging scenarios, such as missing user data and content perturbation. This study highlights the potential of generative AI for optimizing both content creation and marketing performance in digital commerce environments.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students retrieve and consume academic information, yet whether it substitutes for or complements library resources remains contested, and prior surveys rarely separate auxiliary from substitutive use. Methods This study uses a convergent triangulation design that combines multiple quantitative methods. It addresses the same set of research propositions by collecting perceptual-level questionnaire data and behavioral-level logs and platform usage statistics, analyzing them independently, and comparing the findings at the interpretation stage. Using 368 student questionnaires, we test an auxiliary-substitutive dual-path structural equation model and compare the results with an interrupted time-series analysis of 3.2 million print-loan logs (2017-2025) and digital-platform statistics from 2021 to the first half of 2026. Results Print-resource continuance intention is positively associated with deep-reading demand, but not significantly associated with auxiliary GenAI use. Survey results showed auxiliary GenAI use positively associated with digital-resource continuance intention, yet insufficiently distinct from perceived digital-resource convenience; platform data showed nascent use of embedded AI features. Substitutive GenAI use shows only a weak negative association with print-resource continuance intention, while the nine-year loan record reveals no significant level or trend change at the January 2023 breakpoint; task-channel fit shows no significant moderating effect. Discussion In this institution, findings align more with dual-channel coexistence than with the “AI-replaces-libraries” narrative; the survey-level substitution association has not yet appeared in aggregate borrowing behavior, informing collection development, service redesign, and AI-literacy education.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: Aim: To map recent artificial intelligence research in family medicine and primary care against an earlier 2015–2024 bibliometric baseline. Methods: Scopus was searched on 9 July 2026 for 2016–2026 publications. One researcher screened 3452 articles and reviews; 132 topical and 13 language exclusions left 3307 records. Manual title, DOI, and Scopus-identifier checks identified no duplicates. VOSviewer 1.6.21 and Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.4.1; R 4.6.1) supported descriptive analysis and mapping. Results: Output increased from 531 in 2024 to 792 in 2025 (49.2%). The 2025 and partial 2026 component contained 1407 records (42.5%); 615 were dated 2026. The USA led publication and raw citation rankings (711 publications; 18,671 citations), while China preceded the United Kingdom in publication count. The Journal of Medical Internet Research (78 publications) and Scientific Reports (69) led the venues; seven top ten venues were shared with the earlier study. Language model terminology coexisted with later-positioned explainability, risk stratification, and diagnostic accuracy terms. Conclusions: This updated map quantifies post-2024 activity and identifies continuity and corpus-dependent differences in geography, dissemination, and evaluation-related vocabulary. Single-database and English language coverage, single-researcher screening, unadjusted citations, and incomplete 2026 coverage limit inference. The findings describe research activity, not clinical adoption, safety, effectiveness, or causality.

documents.abstract: Se examinó la gobernanza algorítmica aplicada en la administración tributaria ecuatoriana mediante los sistemas Orión y Falcon, con el objetivo de determinar la compatibilidad del uso de inteligencia artificial y analítica de riesgos con la transparencia administrativa, la protección de datos personales y los derechos del contribuyente, se planteó qué garantías jurídicas debieron regir la selección automatizada de casos y la actuación fiscalizadora posterior, el alcance comprendió normativa constitucional, tributaria, administrativa y de protección de datos, documentos institucionales y estándares internacionales, se aplicó un enfoque jurídico cualitativo, documental, analítico y comparado, complementado con una matriz ordinal de doce dimensiones, seis tablas y seis figuras, los resultados evidenciaron información pública parcial sobre finalidad, seguridad y gestión institucional, junto con vacíos sobre variables, validación, explicabilidad, supervisión y auditoría, se concluyó que la legitimidad exigió intervención humana, trazabilidad, evaluación de impacto, transparencia escalonada, contradicción y revisión independiente, con garantías efectivas de defensa. Palabras clave: auditoría algorítmica, debido proceso, explicabilidad, protección de datos, reserva tributaria Abstract Algorithmic governance in Ecuadorian tax administration through the Orion and Falcon systems was examined within a framework of risk-based digital enforcement and constitutional accountability in public decision-making processes affecting taxpayers, to determine whether artificial intelligence and risk analytics were compatible with administrative transparency, personal data protection, and taxpayer rights, the research question addressed which legal safeguards should have governed automated case selection and subsequent audit action, the scope covered constitutional, tax, administrative, and data protection rules, institutional documents, and international standards, a qualitative, documentary, analytical, and comparative legal approach was applied, supplemented by an ordinal matrix of twelve dimensions, six tables, and six figures, the findings showed partial public information on purpose, security, and institutional management, together with gaps concerning variables, validation, explainability, supervision, and auditing, the analysis concluded that legitimacy required meaningful human intervention, traceability, impact assessment, tiered transparency, challenge procedures, independent review, and effective safeguards for defense. Keywords: algorithmic auditing, data protection, due process, explainability, tax secrecy

In this scholarly dialogue for Media, Technology, and Governance , Guilherme Canela reflects on the centrality of governance in contemporary debates over media, technology, and the global information ecosystem. Drawing on his long-standing work with journalists, governments, civil society, regulators, judges, researchers, and international organizations, Canela situates freedom of expression, access to information, and digital transformation within a broader human rights framework. The conversation begins with Canela's professional trajectory from Latin America to UNESCO headquarters in Paris, then turns to the challenges posed by generative artificial intelligence, platform power, journalism's economic viability, and the need for multistakeholder governance. Canela argues that although technologies change, the principles of journalism, human rights, transparency, accountability, and meaningful participation remain essential. He also calls for scholars to study information and journalism as public goods, the growing attacks on accountability systems, and the ways academic evidence can inform policymaking without sacrificing independence. The dialogue concludes with a message to researchers: governance is the key topic of the coming years, and the academic community is needed to provide the evidence, concepts, and critical debate required to meet that challenge.

Clinician-facing artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools can benefit patient care, but also have potential to cause physical or psychological patient harm. Opinions differ among stakeholders on who should be held responsible when such events occur – the clinician, the developer or vendor, the deploying institution, or some combination. Under current Australian tort law, clinicians remain primarily responsible for patient harm, even if software is shown to be flawed. As a result, clinicians may avoid or delay using AI tools despite demonstrated benefits to patient care. We briefly describe unique legal challenges posed by the use of AI tools, propose a framework for sharing liability among all parties according to their contribution to AI-related harm, and, failing this, offer nine strategies that clinicians and health services can adopt now to lower their liability risk.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Green and sustainable computing has evolved from a narrow focus on reducing the energy consumed by computer hardware into a broader discipline concerned with energy efficiency, distributed architectures, artificial intelligence, environmental impact, and lifecycle sustainability. This paper presents a structured review and trend analysis based on the findings reported in a recent large-scale study of 11,119 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 1960 and 2025. The reviewed study used BERTopic with transformer-based embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, and temporal analysis to identify 36 research topics. This paper reorganizes those findings into an IJARSCT-style review format and synthesizes the major research directions, thematic groups, developmental stages, challenges, and future opportunities. The evidence shows that virtualization and hardware-efficiency themes have historically been important, while edge computing, AI-supported systems, neuromorphic architectures, UAV computing, and environmentally aware computation have gained research attention. The review also highlights limitations associated with database coverage, metadata quality, topic interpretation, and the use of relative topic prevalence. The resulting framework can help students and researchers understand the changing landscape of green computing and identify areas for further investigation.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that studies intelligent machine learning, including various advanced tools capable of mimicking human intelligence. AI plays an important role in the research field, especially in new drug discovery. AI can tackle many disciplines, including computer science, psychology, and philosophy. AI can work in various fields including science, technology and the pharmaceutical as well as natural science sector to improve efficacy and productivity. AI is now widely used in many industries and research fields because of the high-performance of computer hardware, ample storage, easily available software, and also be a cost effective. In recent years, the continuous advances in Machine learning (ML) algorithms have led to the development of Deep learning (DL) techniques with stronger capabilities in handling big data, which can further assist in identifying natural products and validation of computer-assisted lead identification. This review mainly summarized the rational application and advantages of AI based models to enhance the drug discovery process, including the Natural drug discovery and optimizing drug structures through ML/DL computational tools.

Background Digital repositories and databases facilitate faster dissemination, transparency, and stakeholder collaboration. This review aimed to map and evaluate such digital infrastructures, focusing on their scope, content, functionality, adherence to FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability and Reuse) principles, and user interface and experiences (UI/UX). Methods A review of global digital health policy repositories was conducted across multiple search engines and databases. The review targeted digital repositories that systematically collate health policy documents at a global level. Two country-specific repositories with a bearing on global health policies were also included. Results The study identified 59 global health policy repositories, with 15 matching our inclusion criteria evaluated in detail. These repositories contain vast amounts of data and are generally freely accessible, rendering them immensely rich sources for health policy documents, though with significant variability in content and coverage. The majority have a health focus, including HIV/AIDS, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH); about a third are broader and more emerging health threats are often neglected. Accessibility and usability are limited, with basic UI features such as search and filtering tools are present for almost all repositories and a notable lack of advanced analytics or artificial intelligence capabilities. Furthermore, many repositories struggle to adhere to FAIR principles, reducing their utility and potential for integration. Sustainability is also a concern, as funding often relies on short-term projects or philanthropic support, undermining long-term viability. Conclusion These issues collectively hinder the ability of digital health policy repositories to support comprehensive and timely global health policy development. To unlock the full potential of existing or new repositories for health policy, identified challenges should be tackled systematically. We provide specific recommendations aimed at driving the development of equitable, inclusive, high-functioning repositories and strengthening evidence-driven global health policy systems.

Higher education is confronting its fourth major disruption within a single career arc, one defined not by a single policy shift or budget crisis but by a deep cultural reckoning. Over the past 30 years, 3 technological revolutions, the Internet, the smartphone, and generative artificial intelligence (AI), have systematically collapsed distance, time, and trust. Rather than transform in response, higher education layered new technologies atop legacy structures, raising costs and eroding public credibility. Today, the sector faces a collapse of legitimacy, fueling political interventions and public skepticism. This chapter argues that surviving and leading through this era requires more than strategic planning or operational efficiency. It demands a posture of resilient, continual crisis leadership grounded in human connection. Drawing from decades of leadership experience across multiple institutions and crises, Timothy Chester offers six practical strategies designed to rebuild trust and guide institutions through ongoing volatility. In an age where disruption is a permanent condition, this chapter serves as both a warning and a field guide, calling leaders to embrace clarity, compassion, and steady presence as higher education navigates its most profound test yet.

AI applications, including virtual patients and conversational agents, offer promising enhancements to communication skills training for pharmacy students, providing interactive and repetitive practice opportunities that traditional methods may lack.
