documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to empirically examine how instructors’ learning facilitation competency and learners’ self-leadership are associated with engagement, satisfaction and transfer in corporate training contexts. It further investigates whether learning engagement mediates the relationships among these key variables. Design/methodology/approach The research was conducted with a sample of 537 adult learners who had prior experience in corporate training programs and was grounded in facilitation learning theory and self-directed learning theory. Findings The findings show that instructors’ facilitation competency is significantly associated with learning engagement and satisfaction but does not show a significant direct relationship with learning transfer. Learners’ self-leadership is positively associated with all three outcomes: engagement, satisfaction and transfer. Learning engagement functions as a key mediator, especially between facilitation competency and transfer. Overall, facilitation competency shows stronger associations with engagement and satisfaction than self-leadership. Research limitations/implications This study has several limitations. First, cross-sectional self-report data limits causal inference and common method bias may inflate associations, particularly for learning transfer. Second, the sample is limited to Korean adult learners, which may affect generalizability across cultural contexts. Third, organizational variables – such as supervisor support, learning climate and transfer opportunities – were not included, though these are known predictors of transfer. Future research should adopt longitudinal or experimental designs, incorporate organizational-level variables, replicate findings across diverse cultural contexts and reexamine discriminant validity between self-leadership and learning engagement. Practical implications Findings suggest that both instructor facilitation and learner self-leadership matter for training effectiveness. Organizations should invest in developing instructors’ facilitation competencies – not just content expertise – to foster engagement and satisfaction. Equally, training programs should be designed to strengthen learners’ self-leadership skills, as these are associated with engagement, satisfaction and transfer. Since learning engagement emerged as a key mediator, instructional strategies that deepen active participation are likely to improve training outcomes. Psychologically safe learning climates and structured instructor development are essential for transfer-oriented instruction. Social implications When instructors move beyond simply delivering content and truly function as learning facilitators, learners develop the capacity to think for themselves, adapt to new challenges and apply what they have learned in meaningful ways. Corporate training must not stop at learning – what matters is whether that learning carries over into practice and shows up in organizational outcomes. By investing in facilitation competency and learner self-leadership, organizations can cultivate workforces capable of continuous adaptation. In an AI-driven era, human facilitation remains irreplaceable for fostering autonomous, transfer-ready learners. Originality/value These results provide empirical support for Rogers’ (1969) assertion that instructors, when functioning as facilitators rather than one-way deliverers of knowledge, foster meaningful learning experiences. Ultimately, this study offers both theoretical and practical implications for improving learner satisfaction and instructional effectiveness in workplace learning contexts.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Skin diseases are common health conditions that affect people worldwide. Early detection and accurate classification of skin diseases are important for supporting timely medical treatment. However, identifying skin diseases through visual examination can be challenging because different skin conditions may have similar visual characteristics. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence and deep learning have created opportunities to develop computer-aided systems for medical image analysis. This research focuses on human skin disease detection using deep learning techniques. The proposed approach uses skin images as input and applies image preprocessing techniques to prepare the images for classification. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can automatically extract important features such as colour, texture, and lesion patterns. Residual Networks (ResNet) can also be used to learn complex image features through their residual connections, supporting the classification of different skin conditions. The system aims to identify patterns in skin images and classify them into predefined disease categories based on the training data. The performance of the proposed approach can be assessed using evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. This research explores the potential of deep learning to support preliminary skin disease screening and improve the efficiency of image-based analysis. The system is intended to assist healthcare professionals and is not a replacement for professional medical diagnosis Keywords— Keywords: Human Skin Disease Detection, Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), ResNet, Image Processing, Skin Lesion Classification, Melanoma Detection, Medical Image Analysis, Transfer Learning, Artificial Intelligence.

Biomechanics is an interdisciplinary field which combines physics, mechanical engineering, and life sciences to understand the relationship of physical forces to the functioning of the human body. A very important concept of biomechanics is that of human tolerance: there are quantifiable limits to the human's ability to withstand physical forces without harm. If these limits are exceeded, reversible or irreversible injury will occur. Vehicles and equipment can be designed such that even if a vehicle is involved in a crash the, resulting injuries are minimized or eliminated. Principles of ergonomics can be used to make equipment easier to use, more efficient, less tiring, and therefore safer.

This study investigates how human-AI collaboration reshapes corporate communication models within intelligent transformation, focusing on university–industry–research collaboration as an enabling mechanism. Drawing on qualitative case evidence and framework development, the paper identifies three collaborative modes-co-design, adaptive integration, and evaluative feedback-that mediate between AI capabilities and organizational communication innovation. The findings suggest that successful intelligent transformation depends less on technology adoption than on the institutional alignment of academic knowledge, industrial practice, and research-driven experimentation. Corporate communication evolves from linear information dissemination to dynamic stakeholder engagement, with human oversight and ethical judgment embedded in AI-supported workflows. The paper contributes a framework linking university–industry–research inputs, human-AI collaboration modes, and communication performance, and concludes with implications for policy and managerial practice.

Clinicians use Large Language Models (LLMs) for clinical decision support, medical question answering, and automated document writing. However, these models can hallucinate and pose safety risks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factuality, it does not always produce outputs consistent with supporting evidence. To address these issues, this study reframes NLI-based unsupported-response rate mitigation for generative models as a confidence-aware inference problem and proposes a unified CARE-Med framework for retrieval, generation, and verification. The framework ensures the reliability of its outputs by leveraging dense retrieval, natural language inference verifiers, and a confidence scoring mechanism. The authors validated the anti-NLI-based unsupported-response optimisation method for biomedical large models proposed in this paper against the MIMIC-III, PubMedQA, and BioASQ benchmarks. The method reduces NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 32% for the Baseline LLM to 10% for CARE-Med, corresponding to a 22-percentage-point or 68.8% relative reduction. Compared with conventional RAG, NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 21% to 10%, corresponding to an 11-percentage-point or 52.4% relative reduction. The authors leverage explicit verification and uncertainty reasoning to meet requirements for safe clinical deployment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: This research aimed to analyze and identify the opportunities and challenges of applying artificial intelligence (AI) in the pre-hospital emergency setting for the diagnosis, initial management, and triage of trauma patients.The objective is to provide a practical roadmap for the policymaking and safe implementation of this technology.Methods: This qualitative study was conducted using a meta-synthesis (research synthesis) approach.A systematic search was performed in major scientific databases to identify original articles published between 2015 and 2026 (1394-1404 in the Iranian calendar).After screening the studies based on the PRISMA guidelines, data from the eligible articles were extracted using a structured checklist and analyzed through thematic content analysis (TCA).The trustworthiness of the findings was assessed and confirmed according to Lincoln and Guba's criteria.Results: Out of a total of 221 retrieved articles, 24 eligible studies were included in the analysis.The findings indicated that AI application, on one hand, possesses significant potential to transform clinical and operational processes.These potentials include enhancing triage accuracy, intelligent patient monitoring, decision support, logistics optimization, and efficient documentation.On the other hand, realizing these opportunities is contingent upon overcoming a wide range of obstacles, including data and information issues, infrastructural and technical limitations, algorithmic constraints, human and organizational barriers, and ethical and legal considerations.Conclusion: Although AI, by enabling intelligent monitoring and improving triage accuracy, has the potential to revolutionize the management of the "golden hour" in trauma care, its implementation is confronted with five multifaceted categories of challenges.The results indicate that the successful translation of these opportunities into sustainable clinical practice cannot be achieved solely through technological advancement; rather, it requires systemic transformation, an integrated approach, and the adoption of evidence-based policies to simultaneously address infrastructural, human, and legal barriers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The authors investigated the impact of Artificial Intelligence on the personalized cosmetic shopping experience on the Shopee e-commerce platform in Viet Nam. The team proposed seven hypotheses examining how AI-related factors influence user satisfaction. A quantitative approach was used, with survey data collected from 229 respondents and analyzed via SPSS 22. Results indicate that five factors - Personalization Risk Management, Perceived Usefulness, Trust Level, Customer Behavior Recognition, and User Data Quality- have significant positive effects on user satisfaction. At the same time, the quality of Machine Learning Algorithms, when applied mechanically without domain-specific calibration, has a statistically significant negative effect. These findings contribute a novel empirical perspective on AI adoption in a high-involvement product category to offer practical recommendations for platform developers, cosmetic sellers, and regulatory authorities.

This research explores the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on medical education, highlighting its applications, benefits, and challenges.AI has revolutionized medical teaching through tools such as advanced clinical simulations, intelligent tutoring systems, AI-assisted diagnostics, and automated assessments.These technologies enable personalized, safe, and efficient learning, enhancing the acquisition of clinical and diagnostic skills.Additionally, immediate feedback and the ability to practice in virtual environments without risking patient safety are significant benefits.However, the implementation of AI faces challenges such as data privacy, high costs, unequal accessibility, and the need for faculty training.The risk of technological dependency and the potential loss of essential soft skills in medical practice are also discussed.The essay concludes that while AI offers transformative opportunities, its integration must be carefully managed to ensure it complements, rather than replaces, human clinical judgment.The importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and ongoing research is emphasized to maximize the benefits of AI in medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose While AI conversational agents such as Woebot offer a promising avenue for improving psychological well-being through empathetic conversations with nonclinical populations, growing privacy breach risks of AI are a significant threat to their use for emotional support. Therefore, this study aims to examine how confidentiality assurances from AI agents affect user satisfaction with AI-assisted emotional support, exploring the serial-mediation effects of perceived confidentiality and self-disclosure and the moderation effect of privacy concerns. Design/methodology/approach In a controlled experiment, 350 US adults interacted with a standardized AI emotional support agent in a three-dimensional metaverse and were randomly assigned to either the confidentiality-assurance condition or the control condition. Findings Results showed that confidentiality assurances significantly increased user satisfaction with AI-assisted emotional support. Moreover, we observed the mediation effects of perceived confidentiality and the serial-mediation effects of both perceived confidentiality and willingness to self-disclose. Originality/value This study contributes to the privacy literature by exploring how brief, standardized confidentiality assurances function in an AI-driven emotional support context. Instead of focusing on complex, personalized privacy designs, these findings offer a nuanced perspective on human-AI interactions that a simple structural cue can serve as a sufficient heuristic anchor to strengthen users' willingness to self-disclose across varying user traits.

Introduction: Firefighters are frequently exposed to traumatic occupational experiences, which may adversely affect their mental health and sleep quality. This study aimed to investigate the effect of a mindfulness-based intervention on post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and sleep quality among firefighters in Shiraz, Iran. Methods: This quasi-experimental study employed a pre-test, post-test, and two-month follow-up design. A convenience sample of 70 male trauma-exposed firefighters was recruited (2023–2024). Participants were assigned to either a mindfulness intervention group (n=31; M_age=32.00±4.10) or a control group (n=34; M_age=30.65±3.59). The intervention group received an eight-session (90 minutes/week) mindfulness program, while the control group received no intervention. Assessments utilized the Mississippi Scale for Combat-Related PTSD (M-PTSD) and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Data were analyzed using MANCOVA and ANCOVA (SPSS v.28). Results: The mindfulness group demonstrated significant improvements in sleep quality (pre- test: 9.61, post-test: 5.10, follow-up: 5.74) and PTSD symptoms (pre-test: 100.29, post-test: 92.97, follow-up: 94.29) compared to the control group (p<0.001). Multivariate and univariate analyses of covariance confirmed that the intervention group exhibited significantly lower adjusted mean scores for both variables at post-test and follow-up. Conclusion: Mindfulness intervention significantly reduced PTSD symptoms and improved sleep quality among firefighters. These findings suggest that mindfulness training is a viable strategy for stress management and mental well-being in this population. Policymakers are encouraged to integrate mindfulness-based programs into occupational health services for firefighters

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Lateral lymph node metastasis (LLNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) significantly impacts PTC prognosis and treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI)-driven integrated model to predict LLNM by combining clinical data, radiomics features, and deep learning-based imaging features. A cohort of 1566 patients was divided into training, validation, and test sets. To indirectly assess LLNM risk based on tumor aggressiveness characteristics, radiomics features were extracted from ultrasound images of the primary thyroid tumor and selected using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression to construct a support vector machine (SVM) model. Clinical variables were used for logistic regression. Deep learning features characterizing the primary thyroid nodule were derived from the TResNet model, and these predictions were integrated into a multimodal model and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. The integrated model outperformed individual models, achieving the highest area under the curve in the training (0.984), validation (0.943), and test (0.951) datasets. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified key predictive factors such as TResNet scores, SVM-based radiomics features, tumor size, location, sex, and thyroglobulin antibody levels. After incorporating the model, the diagnostic accuracy was enhanced for ultrasound physicians at all levels (junior, medium, and senior), with significant improvements in sensitivity, specificity, and confidence. The proposed AI-driven integrated model, which predicts LLNM risk by analyzing primary thyroid tumor characteristics, demonstrated robust predictive performance and clinical utility in LLNM risk stratification for PTC patients. It significantly improves diagnostic accuracy compared to individual models, providing a non-invasive, personalized tool to support clinical decision-making.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Introduction Prison officers in Chile work under highly stressful and dangerous conditions characterized by prison overcrowding, violence, long shifts, and chronic exposure to stress. Shift work and irregular schedules negatively affect sleep quality and contribute to insomnia, which in turn may impair psychological well-being. Despite growing evidence on occupational stress in correctional staff, limited research has examined the relationship between sleep quality, insomnia, and psychological well-being in prison guards. Therefore, this study aimed to assess working conditions, subjective sleep quality, insomnia severity, and psychological well-being among Chilean prison officers. Methods A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted with 43 prison guards from five prisons in the Valparaíso Region, Chile. Instruments included the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), self-ratings of subjective sleep quality and the Ryff Psychological Wellbeing Scale (PWB). Sociodemographic and work-related variables were also analyzed, including sick leave, exposure to violence at work, need for mental health care, perceived organizational support, and energy drink consumption. Results Participants reported low institutional support (60.5%) and frequent sick leave (68.4%). Over one-third considered seeking psychological care (37.2%), and 53.5% reported daily energy drink consumption. Insomnia levels were moderate and clinically relevant (M = 17.87, SD = 0.91), with high dissatisfaction and functional impairment. Psychological well-being was moderate overall (M = 54.84, SD = 16.52), with higher scores in positive relationships and lower scores in environmental mastery and personal growth. No significant association was found between ISI scores and overall or subscale psychological well-being. However, insomnia was positively associated with years at the institution ( p = 0.023, r = 0.349), indicating that longer tenure relates to higher subjective insomnia severity scores. Conclusions Chilean prison officers exhibited clinically significant insomnia, moderate psychological well-being, and low perceived institutional support. Although no significant association was found between insomnia and psychological well-being, insomnia severity increased with years of service. These findings underscore the need to improve working conditions and implement policies that promote occupational health in Chilean prisons. Incorporating a gender perspective in this highly masculinized context is also recommended, as well as further research to enhance psychological well-being.

Purpose This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming service models, workflows, and workforce roles in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. It examines the extent to which AI adoption influences service delivery, professional responsibilities, staff competencies, organizational readiness, and the development of intelligent library workspaces. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative descriptive design based on twenty semi-structured interviews with librarians, information technology staff, and administrative personnel working in academic libraries in Saudi Arabia. Participants were purposively selected based on their direct experience with AI-supported tools and technology-enabled library services. The interview data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's framework to identify patterns relating to AI-tool adoption, service transformation, workforce competencies, staff readiness, and implementation challenges. Findings The findings reveal four interrelated dimensions of AI-driven transformation in academic libraries. First, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent discovery systems, automated search applications, and plagiarism-detection tools are increasingly embedded in routine library operations. Second, AI is contributing to more automated, personalized, responsive, and digitally mediated service models. Third, workforce roles are shifting toward supervisory, analytical, instructional, and technology-mediated responsibilities, increasing the need for competencies in AI literacy, digital skills, data management, system oversight, and evaluation of AI-generated outputs. Fourth, successful implementation is constrained by training gaps, uneven staff readiness, infrastructural and system-integration limitations, concerns about AI reliability, and ethical issues involving privacy, bias, misinformation, and data governance. The findings emphasize the importance of continuous professional development, reliable technological infrastructure, human oversight, and clear institutional governance mechanisms. Originality/value This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on the simultaneous transformation of library services, workflows, workforce competencies, and organizational readiness associated with AI adoption in Saudi Arabian academic libraries. By integrating the perspectives of librarians, IT personnel, and administrative staff, it extends existing research beyond individual AI applications and conceptualizes AI adoption as a broader socio-technical and workforce transformation. The study also offers practical guidance for library managers on AI competency development, responsible human–AI collaboration, organizational readiness, and ethical governance.

Wrong prescriptions are among the most common causes of patient harm that could have been avoided with medication AI assisting the interpretation of possible ambiguous drug names, dosages, frequencies, routes of administration etc. Unclear handwritten prescriptions represent a significant portion of the cases. Standard OCR can digitize prescription images, but cannot verify medication nor return clinically safe interpretations by itself. We introduce MedGuard AI, an RAG-powered AI system to personalize drug identification and patient safety alerts/notifications. The system transforms prescription text to normalized medication identities which are mapped to structured clinical data to power a patient safety use case. An entity extraction model fine-tuned on token classification tasks locates medication mentions. Dictionary-based normalization and fuzzy matching of known brand, generic, and canonical names follow. This process outputs medication candidates that the user must confirm before safety calculations can begin. Allergy, drug-drug interaction, contraindication and other medication checks are processed by deterministic rule-based engines using structured drug knowledge references. A TF-IDF based retriever operating locally augments generated explanations with extracted supporting evidence, limiting hallucinations and improving traceback. The extraction pipeline model was fine-tuned on 1,500 labeled prescriptions, resulting in an F1-score of 0.86 (macro), 0.97(weighted) and 0.98(micro) with a token accuracy of 0.98. The prototype is made of a FastAPI server, ReactJS 19 web frontend, the local retrieval database, constrained LLM deployed for explanation generation with deterministic offline fallback, PDF rendering for export of results, and 17-unit test cases. Separating deterministic parts from generative parts allows higher trust and clinical defensibility.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Over the past several years, digital intraoral scanning has moved from a promising innovation to a routine part of clinical practice. This review summarizes current evidence on the accuracy of contemporary intraoral scanners, examines the technical, clinical and operator-related factors that determine the quality of a digital impression, and outlines the remaining limitations of the method. Particular attention is paid to devices released in 2024–2026 and to embedded artificial intelligence algorithms used both to improve scan quality and to support diagnosis. The analysis is based on recent systematic reviews, meta-analyses and clinical studies.

This paper examines how artificial intelligence could reshape surveillance and social control in North Korea, focusing on Pyongyang. Rather than viewing AI surveillance as a sudden rupture, it conceptualises it as a possible intensification of North Korea’s existing human-centred system, one that already includes household monitoring, workplace surveillance, mobility control, and ideological discipline. Drawing on studies of surveillance and algorithmic governance, and using the city of Urumqi in Xinjiang as an empirical reference architecture, the paper distinguishes three functions of AI-enabled surveillance: tracking, profiling, and pre-emptive policing. Using scenario analysis, the study identifies two critical uncertainties for the North Korean authorities: the level of domestic technological capacity and access to surveillance-relevant hardware, software, and expertise. It then constructs four potential scenarios for Pyongyang by 2035: the deployment of ‘symbolic’ AI, a constrained deployment of domestic AI, an import-dependent uptake, and a full AI panopticon. The paper argues that the most plausible near-term trajectory is a fragmented, import-dependent expansion of tracking and selective profiling rather than fully integrated predictive control. Despite their fragmentary nature, such systems could increase the costs for North Korean citizens engaging in unauthorised mobility, foreign media circulation, informal economic activity, and local non-compliance, while remaining constrained by energy shortages, fragmented data, bureaucratic silos, and everyday strategies of circumvention.

documents.abstract: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support. By isolating qualitative LLM reasoning from visual perceptual noise and database metadata sparsity, the system successfully bridges the gap between intuitive meal perception and point-of-care dietary risk triage, offering a non-invasive and scalable solution for automated dietary auditing and longitudinal population health monitoring.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has made legal practice easier, especially when it comes to drafting agreements. AI can be used to identify hazards, generate terms, examine contracts, and offer suggestions about the content of contracts. But using AI also brings up legal questions about the legality of contracts, the legal standing of AI, and the parties' liabilities. In accordance with Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code, this study will examine the legality of contracts that incorporate AI. It will also examine the current state of AI and the effects of its application on the parties' rights, responsibilities, and liabilities under Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code. Legal materials are evaluated using a descriptive-qualitative method, and the study uses a normative-juridical approach that makes use of statutory and conceptual approaches. The results show that, as long as the four conditions for a legal agreement are satisfied, the employment of AI does not automatically make an agreement void. While humans or legal entities acting as legal subjects retain power, binding force, and legal culpability, AI is better viewed as an assisting tool. Therefore, in order to guaranty legal certainty and the protection of the parties involved, the deployment of AI necessitates human evaluation and monitoring.

Abstract The exponential deployment of large language models (LLMs) across commercial and public sectors in 2026 and beyond has created an urgent accountability gap that traditional IP frameworks were never designed to address. When these systems generate hallucinations around resultant data in the form of fabricated citations, non-existent precedents, or fictional technical specifications, the resulting misinformation doesn't merely distort discourse but creates chaos to perform the task again from scratch. Factually incorrect output data currently pose significant risks across critical domains including healthcare, legal systems, financial services, and public policy. The hallucination crisis forces us to confront a deeper question: what does it mean to build "responsible" technology when our most advanced creations confidently lie? Through the Khastgir Algorithm's 103 sub-modules, I've always argued that responsibility isn't a compliance checkbox but a living system of interlocking accountabilities—IP rights protecting human creativity, carbon-negative operations preserving planetary boundaries, and DAO governance ensuring no single entity monopolizes truth. Hallucinations expose the moral vacuum in models trained without such frameworks. The current expanded architecture discussed in this paper therefore treats each fabricated output as a teachable moment and not merely flagged and logged, but routed through a global network of stakeholder DAOs who collectively determine the remediation protocol, transforming error correction into a democratic exercise that strengthens rather than erodes public trust in AI systems. This paper expands the foundational Khastgir Algorithm originally designed for AI-mediated intellectual property dispute resolution and time is apt to incorporate Digital Development Goals (DDGs) as one of the governing frameworks for identifying and reporting hallucinated data in real-time. The enhanced comprehensive architecture framework integrates token-level hallucination probes, blockchain-anchored verification mechanisms, and automated reporting pipelines aligned with UNDP's Digital Strategy 2022-2025 objectives and United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The proposed framework leverages advanced machine learning techniques including attention mechanism analysis, semantic consistency validation, and cross-reference verification, combined with a permissioned blockchain architecture running on the Impula Network. Keywords: Hallucination detection, blockchain, artificial intelligence governance, real-time validation, edge computing, digital development goals, ITU-T X.1819, zero-knowledge proofs, Impula Network, Industry 4.0
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to map the intellectual structure, knowledge flows and thematic evolution of cross-buying and customer relationship expansion research in digital retail and service encounter contexts from 2000 to 2026. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric science-mapping design guided by the SPAR-4-SLR protocol was adopted. Data were retrieved from Scopus using a TITLE-ABS-KEY search. After applying year, subject area, document type, language and source type filters and removing one duplicate DOI record, the final data set comprised 567 Scopus-indexed journal documents. “Bibliometrix” and “VOSviewer” were used for performance analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence, temporal overlay, thematic mapping and thematic evolution. Findings The field is rooted in customer lifetime value, customer equity, CRM, service quality, satisfaction, loyalty and relationship marketing. Recent research fronts increasingly emphasise digital service quality, customer engagement, e-commerce, omnichannel service encounters, artificial intelligence, machine learning and predictive analytics. Thematic evolution shows a shift from firm-centric customer valuation and retention models toward digitally mediated, experience-driven and analytics-enabled relationship expansion. Practical implications Managers should treat cross-buying as a relationship-expansion outcome shaped by service quality, trust, customer experience, engagement and responsible data use, rather than only as a sales or targeting objective. Originality/value This study positions cross-buying within customer relationship expansion and provides an integrated bibliometric synthesis of its intellectual foundations, research fronts, conceptual themes and future research agenda.

El discurso dominante sobre la inteligencia artificial en el sector publicitario presenta una disyuntiva simple: las agencias que adopten IA crecerán y las que no, desaparecerán. La evidencia pública de 2024–2026 —comunicaciones de resultados, documentos de registro corporativos, planes y objetivos anunciados, documentación de las plataformas y prensa especializada— no sostiene esa lectura. Este working paper descompone la cadena de valor de la agencia en seis capas —investigación, estrategia, producción creativa, compra de medios, medición y gobernanza— y sostiene que la comoditización avanza capa a capa según tres atributos de cada tarea: si el entregable es especificable, si existe un oráculo de aceptación barato y si la acción es reversible. Definimos operativamente la comoditización como la sustitución de horas facturables por un coste marginal cercano a cero, y mostramos que la parte de la cadena que cumple los tres atributos —variantes creativas, informes, operación de pujas— no la está absorbiendo primero el agente de la agencia, sino la propia plataforma publicitaria, con productos anteriores a la ola de agentes: Meta desplegó su motor de recuperación y clasificación Andromeda en diciembre de 2024, con un aumento declarado de capacidad de modelo de 10 000× y un incremento de ROAS del 22 % reportado por la propia compañía [10]; TikTok lanzó su suite automatizada Smart+ el 7 de octubre de 2024 [11]; y Google elevó en marzo de 2025 el límite de palabras clave negativas de Performance Max a 10 000 por campaña, dejando el límite de cuenta en 1 000 [12]. El hallazgo central es negativo y afecta a la narrativa del sector: la divergencia financiera entre holdings —Publicis con un margen operativo del 18,0 % y un crecimiento orgánico del 5,8 % en 2024 [2], Havas con un crecimiento orgánico del 3,1 % y un margen EBIT ajustado del 12,9 % en 2025 [8], frente a WPP con ingresos menos costes repercutidos de 10 176 millones de libras, un −5,4 % comparable y un deterioro de fondo de comercio de 641 millones [3], Dentsu con un deterioro de 86 000 millones de yenes en el primer semestre de 2025 [6] y un recorte de en torno al 8 % de su plantilla internacional (unos 3 400 empleos) [7], y Omnicom con un objetivo de sinergias elevado a 1 500 millones de dólares tras absorber IPG [5]— no permite identificar el efecto de la adopción de IA. La composición del negocio y las operaciones corporativas son factores concurrentes cuya contribución no se estima aquí. Declaramos explícitamente que con la evidencia pública disponible no es posible separar el efecto de la IA del efecto de las fusiones, los deterioros contables y la pérdida de cuentas: es la limitación más seria de este trabajo y condiciona toda lectura causal. En el lado del consumidor, dos estudios independientes apuntan en la misma dirección —menor resonancia emocional y menor disposición a interactuar cuando se revela el origen sintético [16], [17]—, sin una magnitud del efecto cotejada en esta síntesis. Proponemos una matriz de delegación por capa, una reformulación del modelo de precios acotada por la brecha de atribución (la distancia entre el resultado que la agencia puede medir de forma creíble y el resultado por el que quiere cobrar) y una traducción de la gobernanza de marca a política ejecutable dentro del harness del agente. No aportamos experimento propio ni datos de adopción: el corpus utilizado no contiene telemetría comparable que permita identificar ese tratamiento. Palabras clave: comoditización por capas, cadena de valor de la agencia, agentes LLM en operaciones, Performance Max, Advantage+, modelización de mezcla de marketing, medición incremental, brecha de atribución, gobernanza de marca ejecutable, régimen post-cookie. English abstract: The dominant narrative about artificial intelligence in the advertising industry offers a simple dichotomy: agencies that adopt AI will grow, and those that do not will disappear. Public 2024–2026 evidence —results communications, corporate registration documents, announced plans and targets, platform documentation and trade press— does not support that reading. This working paper decomposes the agency value chain into six layers — research, strategy, creative production, media buying, measurement and governance — and argues that commoditization advances layer by layer according to three task attributes: whether the deliverable is specifiable, whether a cheap acceptance oracle exists, and whether the action is reversible. We define commoditization operationally as the substitution of billable hours by a near-zero marginal cost, and show that the portion of the chain satisfying all three attributes — creative variants, reporting, bid operation — is being absorbed first not by the agency's agent but by the advertising platform itself, through products that predate the agentic wave: Meta deployed its Andromeda retrieval and ranking engine in December 2024, with a declared 10,000× model-capacity increase and a self-reported 22% ROAS lift [10]; TikTok launched its automated Smart+ suite on 7 October 2024 [11]; and Google raised the Performance Max negative-keyword limit to 10,000 per campaign in March 2025, leaving the account-level limit at 1,000 [12]. The central finding is negative and cuts against the industry narrative: financial divergence among holding companies — Publicis at an 18.0% operating margin and 5.8% organic growth in 2024 [2], Havas at 3.1% organic growth and a 12.9% adjusted EBIT margin in 2025 [8], versus WPP with revenue less pass-through costs of £10,176m, −5.4% like-for-like and a £641m goodwill impairment [3], Dentsu with an ¥86bn impairment in the first half of 2025 [6] and a reduction of about 8% of its international workforce (some 3,400 roles) [7], and Omnicom with a synergy target raised to USD 1.5bn after absorbing IPG [5] — does not identify the effect of AI adoption. Business composition and corporate operations are concurrent factors whose contributions are not estimated here. We state explicitly that available public evidence cannot separate the effect of AI from the effects of mergers, accounting impairments and account losses: this is the paper's most serious limitation and it constrains every causal reading. On the consumer side, two independent studies point the same way — lower emotional resonance and lower willingness to engage when synthetic origin is disclosed [16], [17] — without an effect-size estimate verified in this synthesis. We propose a per-layer delegation matrix, a pricing model bounded by the attribution gap (the distance between the outcome an agency can credibly measure and the outcome it wishes to be paid for), and a translation of brand governance into executable policy inside the agent harness. We contribute no original experiment and no adoption data: the corpus used contains no comparable telemetry that identifies that treatment. Keywords: layered commoditization, agency value chain, LLM agents in operations, Performance Max, Advantage+, marketing mix modeling, incrementality measurement, attribution gap, executable brand governance, post-cookie regime. Résumé L’intégration croissante de l’intelligence artificielle dans les systèmes d’information transforme le traitement et l’exploitation des données, tout en exposant les organisations à de nouveaux risques techniques, réglementaires et sociotechniques. La gestion de ces risques constitue ainsi un enjeu important pour une utilisation sûre et responsable de ces technologies. Cette étude vise à examiner comment les organisations peuvent identifier, évaluer et maîtriser les risques liés à l’intelligence artificielle en articulant les dimensions techniques, réglementaires et sociotechniques, souvent abordées séparément. L’étude repose sur une synthèse narrative de la littérature récente. L’analyse est organisée autour de trois ensembles de travaux portant sur les vulnérabilités techniques et les mécanismes de défense, la gouvernance de l’intelligence artificielle et la conformité réglementaire, ainsi que les risques sociotechniques et éthiques. Les résultats montrent que les réponses techniques réduisent certaines vulnérabilités sans garantir une protection durable face à l’évolution des menaces et peuvent entraîner des arbitrages, notamment en matière de confidentialité. Les cadres de gouvernance offrent des repères importants, mais leur mise en œuvre organisationnelle demeure complexe. Les risques sociotechniques restent, quant à eux, insuffisamment intégrés aux processus d’évaluation et de décision. L’étude met en évidence une fragmentation persistante entre ces différentes approches. Elle souligne l’intérêt d’une approche intégrée de la gestion des risques, associant l’évaluation continue des vulnérabilités, une gouvernance adaptée au niveau de risque, la conformité réglementaire et la prise en compte des conséquences sociotechniques dans les systèmes d’information. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; gestion des risques ; gouvernance de l’IA ; systèmes d’information ; conformité réglementaire ; risques sociotechniques. Abstract The growing integration of artificial intelligence into information systems is transforming the processing and use of data while exposing organizations to new technical, regulatory, and sociotechnical risks. Managing these risks has therefore become an important challenge for the safe and responsible use of these technologies. This study examines how organizations can identify, assess, and manage the risks associated with artificial intelligence by bringing together technical, regulatory, and sociotechnical dimensions that are often addressed separately. The study is based on a narrative review of recent literature. The analysis is structured around three main areas: technical vulnerabilities and defense mechanisms, artificial intelligence governance and regulatory compliance, and sociotechnical and ethical risks. The findings show that technical responses can reduce certain vulnerabilities without ensuring lasting protection against evolving threats and may involve trade-offs, particularly regarding privacy. Governance frameworks provide important guidance, but their implementation within organizations remains challenging. Meanwhile, sociotechnical risks are still insufficiently integrated into risk assessment and decision-making processes. The study highlights persistent fragmentation among these approaches. It underlines the value of an integrated risk management approach combining continuous vulnerability assessment, risk-proportionate governance, regulatory compliance, and consideration of sociotechnical consequences within information systems. Keywords : artificial intelligence; risk management; artificial intelligence governance; information systems; regulatory compliance; sociotechnical risks.

documents.abstract: La transformación digital plantea nuevas exigencias para la formación del capital humano corporativo y evidencia limitaciones en las estrategias tradicionales de capacitación frente a las necesidades de aprendizaje ágil, colaborativo y personalizado del entorno empresarial contemporáneo. En este contexto, la convergencia entre inteligencia artificial (IA) y gamificación constituye una alternativa innovadora para fortalecer los procesos de formación. El presente estudio analiza el impacto de la IA en la innovación de procesos, con énfasis en la aplicación de la gamificación y las experiencias inmersivas como estrategias para la capacitación y la optimización del aprendizaje. Se presenta un estudio de caso aplicado a una entidad financiera de Quito, Ecuador, mediante un serious game orientado al fortalecimiento de la cultura organizacional a través de dinámicas colaborativas. Se empleó un enfoque metodológico mixto, basado en entrevistas semiestructuradas, análisis documental, observación de entornos y pruebas de aplicabilidad. Los resultados evidencian un alto nivel de acceso técnico y usabilidad inicial, dado que la mayoría de los participantes logró acceder, instalar e interactuar con la aplicación sin inconvenientes significativos. No obstante, se identificó una brecha entre la autopercepción de los participantes y su desempeño real durante la dinámica del juego. Se concluye que, aunque la gamificación apoyada por IA presenta viabilidad técnica, requiere mejoras en el diseño comunicacional y pedagógico para favorecer la comprensión de los roles y la colaboración efectiva. El estudio aporta evidencia sobre esta brecha y orientaciones para el diseño de serious games aplicados a la formación corporativa. Para explicar la brecha identificada, se proponen tres métricas exploratorias: Perception–Performance Gap (PPG), Behavioral Calibration Ratio (BCR) y Technical–Pedagogical Drop (TPD). Palabra clave: gamificación, innovación tecnológica, inteligencia artificial, negocios Abstract Digital transformation poses new demands on corporate human capital development and highlights limitations in traditional training strategies in addressing the need for agile, collaborative, and personalized learning in the contemporary business environment. In this context, the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and gamification represents an innovative alternative for strengthening training processes. This study analyzes the impact of AI on process innovation, with an emphasis on the application of gamification and immersive experiences as strategies for training and learning optimization. A case study was conducted in a financial institution in Quito, Ecuador, using a serious game aimed at strengthening organizational culture through collaborative dynamics. A mixed-methods approach was employed, based on semi-structured interviews, document analysis, environmental observation, and applicability testing. The results indicate a high level of initial technical access and usability, as most participants were able to access, install, and interact with the application without significant difficulties. However, a gap was identified between participants’ self-perception and their actual performance during the game dynamics. The study concludes that, although AI-supported gamification demonstrates technical feasibility, improvements in communicational and pedagogical design are required to promote role comprehension and effective collaboration. The study provides evidence of this gap and offers guidelines for the design of serious games applied to corporate training. To explain the identified gap, three exploratory metrics are proposed: Perception–Performance Gap (PPG), Behavioral Calibration Ratio (BCR), and Technical–Pedagogical Drop (TPD). Keywords: artificial intelligence, gamification, corporate training, serious games, business innovation

Abstract While language is central to human communication, psychological science has relied on self-reported rating scales for decades because it was difficult to quantify language effectively. Large language models (LLMs) have changed that in recent years. Here, we used LLMs with machine learning to compare traditional ratings against language-based responses (short essays and descriptive words) of experienced well-being over 12 weeks from 764 individuals from an overburdened population highly exposed to emotional experience, U.S. hospitality workers. While accuracies were comparable by internal criterion (across 9 affective traits; words r = .53 vs. .51 for ratings), both language formats doubled the ratings’ accuracy (up to r = .18 and .24 for words and essays, respectively) across 24 external criteria: traits, demographics, and behavior. Beyond improved accuracy, language responses offered psychological insights: words provided concise emotional nuances, whereas essays encompassed broad life contexts. Though each language-based format differed in strengths and weaknesses, both demonstrated greater information-richness than traditional rating scales.

This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing public transit user satisfaction by processing unstructured, voice-derived trip chain data. Traditional survey methods often do not capture the contextual and real time aspects of user experience. To address this limitation, this study employs large language models and natural language processing techniques to analyze trip-related feedback collected from 5,000 public transit users. Sentiment scores were extracted from a station-labeled subset of the data set and applied to a broader corpus to assess satisfaction levels across subway stations in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Using a combination of sentiment analysis and K-means clustering, this study categorized 102 subway stations into three groups: (1) High Satisfaction Station Group; (2) Low Satisfaction Station Group; and (3) Moderate Satisfaction Station Group. These clusters were the basis for grouping stations, and user feedback on transit experiences was summarized for each station within its respective cluster. This approach enables the identification of low-satisfaction transit stations requiring immediate attention, as well as moderate-satisfaction transit stations where service equity must be addressed. The proposed methodology offers a practical alternative to traditional survey-based assessments by leveraging unstructured public transit users’ data. With further refinement and institutional support, this approach can enhance data-driven, user-centered transit planning and contribute to broader improvements in urban mobility.

ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into medical education, research, and clinical decision‐support applications; however, their ability to apply anatomical knowledge in clinically relevant surgical scenarios remains insufficiently studied. This study evaluated and compared the performance of six contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, and Manus) using 25 expert‐derived applied surgical anatomy scenarios relevant to plastic surgery. Scenarios were developed by an expert panel consisting of one associate professor of anatomy and two plastic surgeons. Responses were generated using a standardized prompt and assessed with a structured scoring rubric evaluating anatomical accuracy, clinical reasoning, completeness, and safety, with a maximum score of 10 points per question. Critical errors were additionally assessed. Significant differences in overall performance were observed among models (Friedman χ 2 = 43.51, p < 0.001). ChatGPT achieved the maximum aggregate score (250/250), followed by Gemini (248/250), DeepSeek (241/250), Copilot (240/250), Claude (235/250), and Manus (219/250). Critical errors were infrequent and were confined to a reconstructive vascular physiology scenario: DeepSeek, Claude, and Manus each demonstrated one observed critical error, whereas ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot demonstrated none. Although all evaluated models demonstrated excellent performance, clinically significant anatomical misconceptions persisted despite high aggregate scores. These findings demonstrate strong performance by the tested LLMs on this specific scenario‐based benchmark, while also identifying clinically meaningful anatomical errors in a subset of responses. Future evaluations should focus not only on overall accuracy but also on clinically meaningful error patterns that may influence surgical decision‐making. Importantly, substantial ceiling effects limited discrimination among high‐performing models, and the findings should therefore be interpreted as performance on this specific benchmark rather than as evidence of a general hierarchy of anatomical reasoning capability.

documents.abstract: Background . Large language models are considered a promising tool for personalized oncology; however, their role in the analysis of molecular data and treatment selection should be clearly distinguished from the functions of specialized predictive models. Objective . To systematize the potential applications of large language models in personalized oncology, primarily for the interpretation of clinical, genomic, and transcriptomic data and of predictions of tumor chemo- and radiosensitivity. Methods . We performed a narrative review of publications identified in PubMed and Google Scholar, with the search updated through July 1, 2026. Original studies and reviews on medical LLM applications, foundation models for genomic and transcriptomic data, clinical decision support, and prediction of anticancer treatment sensitivity were considered. Results . The most justified approach is to use a language model as an interface layer: a specialized machine-learning or deep-learning model calculates the prediction, while the language model generates an explanation, compares the result with clinical guidelines, and indicates limitations. The main risks include unreliable responses, insufficient reproducibility, weak external validation, and legal constraints. Conclusion . A clinically promising architecture separates computation from explanation: the language model does not prescribe treatment autonomously but links molecular data, a validated predictive model, and the physician.

documents.abstract: Modern organizational leaders increasingly encounter artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in their workplaces, creating both opportunities and challenges for inclusive leadership. This chapter introduces Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as a framework for navigating these technological changes while maintaining human-centered approaches to inclusion. UDL’s three core principles – multiple means of representation, engagement, and action/expression – provide leaders with practical strategies for creating flexible workplace systems that benefit all employees. When thoughtfully implemented, AI technologies can support these principles through personalized learning experiences, enhanced accessibility features, and improved communication tools. However, the chapter cautions leaders to ensure that technology is amplifying rather than replacing human judgment and cultural competence. The chapter addresses critical considerations for leaders, including the risks of algorithmic bias, the limitations of automated solutions in complex interpersonal situations, and the importance of maintaining employee agency and choice. It examines common implementation barriers – from cost concerns to misconceptions about technology as a cure-all for inclusion challenges – while demonstrating that UDL principles require minimal investment and generate significant returns. Through examination of both opportunities and pitfalls, leaders learn to distinguish between technological applications that enhance inclusion and those that may inadvertently create barriers. The chapter provides actionable guidance for implementing UDL principles in technology-enhanced environments, positioning inclusive leadership capabilities as essential competencies for organizational success regardless of technological context.

documents.abstract: The paper examines the conceptual foundations of the legal regulation of artificial intelligence and the possibilities of their application to the education system. The initial premise of the work is the proposition that AI has ceased to be a private technical instrument and has turned into an infrastructural technology that defines a new socio-political era and generates constitutional challenges of a systemic, synergetic and existential nature. The author identifies the key threats: the substitution of democratic institutions by algorithmic governance, technologically conditioned inequality and algorithmic discrimination, micro-manipulation of the information flow, and the concentration of power resources among the holders of algorithms. As a meta-threat, the challenge to the socio-humanistic paradigm is considered, associated with the choice between transhumanism and classical humanism. By way of discussion, eight principles of the legal regulation of AI are formulated: state strategic guidance and technological integrity; guaranteed protection of the affected person and enhanced liability; "human in the loop" in critical decisions; anthropological priority; digital equality and the prohibition of discrimination; respect for dignity and non-interference in the private sphere; managed transparency; technological neutrality and anticipatory regulation. Further, these principles are projected onto the sphere of education. The author distinguishes two modalities of the use of AI — "a simulator for the mind" and "a prosthesis for laziness" — and shows that legal regulation must establish the boundaries of the permissible application of the technology. The legal risks of algorithmic assessment are analyzed, along with the problem of the right to explanation and the protection of the student from unfounded accusations, digital inequality in access to AI tools, threats to privacy and dignity, as well as the question of the status of the educator as a condition for the humanistic development of AI. A conclusion is drawn regarding the necessity of building a system of requirements for transparency, accountability, equality of access and the preservation of human control in critical decisions.

documents.abstract: Cross-border mobility and career pivoting represent high-stakes, multi-variable optimization challenges traditionally hindered by qualitative ambiguity, subjective counseling, and disconnected legal-financial silos. In this paper, we introduce LifeUML, a formal, declarative domain-specific language (DSL) and deterministic mathematical formulation engineered to model human life trajectories, cross-border solvency runway, and global immigration feasibility. Inspired by the declarative abstraction paradigms of UML and PlantUML, LifeUML enables autonomous AI agents and individuals to compile human aspirations into structured Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) that are evaluated in-browser against empirical psychometrics (IPIP Big-Five, Holland RIASEC) and verified 2026 sovereign statutory immigration gazettes across 40 jurisdictions. We formalize four core computational metrics: (1) the Life Mobility Index (LMI), evaluating legal solvency margins, emergency cash runways, fiscal retention, and cross-cultural adaptability; (2) the AI Transformation Quotient (AX-Q), quantifying autonomous digital leverage; (3) the Dream Convergence Index (DCI), modeling high-dimensional cosine aptitude alignment against target innovation clusters; and (4) an exponential temporal willpower decay model (C(t) = C0 * exp(-lambda * t)) that enforces deterministic action-locking. We further delineate comprehensive legal and ethical safeguards: a clean-room TypeScript parser ensuring copyright independence, public-domain psychometric foundations that bypass proprietary trademark liabilities, statutory delta calculations that prevent the unauthorized practice of law (UPL), and zero-server client-side execution complying with EU AI Act (2024/1689) high-risk employment exemptions.

Digital literacy has become an important competence for university students writing academic papers, particularly in the final semester when they prepare articles, research proposals, or undergraduate theses. Digital literacy involves more than operating devices; it also includes searching for information, evaluating source credibility, managing references, composing texts, and using technology ethically. This article examines how digital literacy supports the academic writing skills of eighth-semester students through a literature review. A narrative literature review was conducted by examining relevant journal articles available online. Sources were selected based on topical relevance, their connection to higher education students, and the availability of bibliographic information and accessible abstracts or full texts. The review indicates that digital literacy supports writing through access to scholarly sources, information evaluation, the use of word-processing and reference-management applications, and more efficient revision. These benefits, however, require critical thinking, knowledge of academic conventions, and ethical technology use, including the use of artificial intelligence. Therefore, digital literacy development should be integrated with reading habits, writing practice, lecturer guidance, and academic integrity.

The materials include questionnaires, an evaluated report example, a codebook, aggregate study results, and supporting prompt and configuration information. documents.abstract: The increasing use of machine learning (ML) in privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and user-facing services has intensified the need for techniques that enable data-driven intelligence without exposing sensitive information. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) offers a cryptographically rigorous approach to privacy-preserving machine learning by allowing computations to be performed directly on encrypted data. While appealing in principle, the integration of FHE into modern ML pipelines introduces substantial challenges that fundamentally affect model design, algorithm selection, and system performance. This survey provides a comprehensive and structured review of machine learning over encrypted data using non-interactive FHE-based approaches. We examine how a wide range of machine learning models, including traditional ML algorithms, deep neural networks, and emerging transformer architectures, are adapted to operate under the arithmetic, precision, and efficiency constraints imposed by FHE. To organize a rapidly growing body of work, we introduce a unifying taxonomy that captures key design dimensions such as encryption schemes, nonlinearity handling strategies, model families, system-level optimizations, and privacy objectives. Using this framework, we synthesize existing approaches, analyze trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and security, and highlight recurring design patterns across the literature. Beyond summarizing existing techniques, this survey discusses practical limitations, deployment considerations, and open research challenges that shape the future of privacy-preserving machine learning under encryption. By bridging cryptographic techniques and modern AI system design, this work aims to serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop secure, scalable, and trustworthy machine learning systems.

Background Machine learning-based assessment of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) has been proposed to improve the reproducibility and clinical utility of immune-contexture evaluation in breast cancer histopathology. However, existing studies differ substantially in task definition, annotation strategy, model architecture, validation design, and clinical endpoint. This systematic review and evidence-gap analysis aimed to map the translational readiness of TIL-related machine learning studies in breast cancer histopathology and to identify cluster-specific methodological gaps. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar was conducted up to 20 April 2026, supplemented by backward citation tracing and a targeted Google search of the 30 most relevant additional results. Eligible studies included breast cancer histopathology-based machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, or computational image-analysis studies evaluating TILs or TIL-related immune-cell features. Studies were grouped by principal application into detection/classification, outcome prognostication, and treatment-response prediction. Extracted variables included data source, specimen type, model family, annotation strategy, validation design, clinical comparator use, calibration, decision-curve analysis, incremental value, reproducibility, and methodological challenges. Because of heterogeneity in endpoints and performance metrics, synthesis was descriptive and evidence-map based. Results The primary evidence map included 51 histopathology-image studies: 19 detection/classification, 18 outcome prognostication, and 14 treatment-response prediction studies. External validation was reported in 31.6% of detection/classification studies, 61.1% of prognostication studies, and 57.1% of treatment-response prediction studies. Clinical comparator reporting increased across the same continuum, from 63.2% to 94.4% and 92.9%, respectively. However, calibration was reported in only one prognostication study (5.6%) and in no detection/classification or treatment-response prediction studies. Decision-curve analysis was similarly limited to one prognostication study. Class imbalance was near-universal (94.7–100% across clusters). Scanner/stain robustness was addressed in a majority of studies (63.2–83.3%), but fairness or subgroup analyses remained inconsistently reported (27.8–57.1%). Conclusions TIL machine learning in breast cancer is technically active but clinically under-validated. Future studies should move beyond model development toward externally validated, calibrated, clinically benchmarked, reproducible, and decision-relevant evidence, using cluster-specific planning standards for detection, prognostication, and treatment-response prediction. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024574566 , identifier CRD42024574566.

documents.abstract: Real-time dashboards were one of the emblematic features of the COVID-19 pandemic. This article analyses dashboards as popular media of situational awareness. After developing an analytics of the popular inspired by systems theory and deconstruction, we highlight three points. First, the proliferation of the dashboard can be understood against the backdrop of a liberal biopolitics of health emergencies. Under liberal conditions, public health officials depend on the cooperation of the population, which is why communicating the situation is a central element of crisis management in pandemics. Second, the dashboard can be understood as a technical solution to the communication challenges associated with lay audiences. From the perspective of those responsible, laypeople have difficulty correctly interpreting scientific data on the pandemic, which is why alternative forms of representation and communication are needed. Finally, we highlight the affective dimension of dashboard inclusion. The aesthetic of the dashboard is observed as an affective tool that is capable of fascinating the public even before any meaning is processed. On the one hand, this fascination fosters inclusion, as it binds the viewer more strongly to the events. However, it also becomes problematic when aesthetic dramatization threatens to undermine the subjectification of a pandemic citizenship.

Research on institutional change in higher education has grown quickly, but it remains fragmented across disciplines and theoretical traditions. This study maps the thematic structure of this research in educational sciences and traces how it has changed over 34 years. I analysed the titles and abstracts of 2,623 publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (Education & Educational Research, 1992–2025) with BERTopic, an embedding-based topic modelling tool. Placeholder masking kept the names of countries, nationalities and languages from shaping the topics, and key model settings are reported for reproducibility. The model produced 24 interpretable topics covering 1,824 publications. The general Structural Reforms topic fell from 65.6% of topic-assigned publications in 1992–2000 to 12.5% in 2023–2025, while more specific themes such as sustainability, transformational leadership and diversity, equity and inclusion gained weight. In 2023–2025, Digital Transformation became the largest topic (14.8%), and Artificial Intelligence Integration rose from almost zero to 8.1%. Technology-related research developed in successive waves: e-learning, emergency remote teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, digital transformation and generative artificial intelligence. Each wave reframed digitalisation with new concepts instead of simply continuing the previous one. These results suggest that institutional change in higher education is studied through several parallel pathways rather than a single dominant narrative. For policymakers and institutional leaders, the findings point to the need to build the capacity for change as a lasting institutional capability rather than responding to each technological, sociological and political disruption separately.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant potential to accelerate drug discovery, yet its adoption remains constrained by interdependent technical, organizational, and regulatory barriers. This study applies Fuzzy DEMATEL to analyze twelve challenges and uncover their causal structure using expert judgments expressed as triangular fuzzy numbers. Following normalization and CFCS defuzzification, Resistance to Change, Lack of Standardization, Limited Trust in AI Outputs, Talent Shortage, and Lack of Clinical Validation emerge as the primary causal drivers. These upstream barriers exert strong influence on downstream effects, including Regulatory Barriers, Biological Complexity, Integration with Legacy Systems, and Poor Data Quality. The findings indicate that several constraints commonly viewed as external are, in practice, manifestations of internal organizational and technical shortcomings. By providing a structured causal prioritization of barriers, this study offers actionable guidance for targeting high-leverage interventions in AI-enabled drug discovery. Findings reflect expert judgment within a North Cyprus context and should be interpreted as indicative organizational signals rather than universal prescriptions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in atmospheric aerosol and particulate-matter (PM) research because it can model nonlinear relationships, integrate heterogeneous observations, and generate high-resolution spatiotemporal information. This study maps the evolution and knowledge structure of AI-based atmospheric aerosol and PM research using 4,872 Web of Science (WoS) publications published through December 31, 2025. Bibliometric and text-mining analyses were used to characterize publication trends, leading countries and institutions, major journals, citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence networks, and abstract-based thematic clusters. In addition, 99 publications indexed in the Korea Citation Index (KCI) were examined separately to provide supplementary context on temporal publication trends in the Korean domestic literature. WoS publication activity increased sharply after 2019, with China contributing the largest publication output and total citation count, while several lower-output countries showed higher mean citations per publication. Keyword-network analysis identified machine learning as a central theme linking PM prediction, deep learning, aerosol optical depth, exposure assessment, and satellite remote sensing. Abstract-based clustering revealed five major thematic domains spanning prediction modeling, PM concentration and exposure, satellite-based aerosol retrieval, emission-related analysis, and aerosol monitoring and environmental applications. The results indicate a shift from model-specific prediction toward multisource integration, spatiotemporal analysis, remote sensing, and exposure-oriented applications. These findings provide a structured overview of the field and highlight the need for more interpretable, uncertainty-aware, and transferable AI approaches.

This study aimed to examine how mathematics teachers in public schools in Türkiye evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics teaching. The accuracy and pedagogical suitability of AI-generated content make such judgments important in mathematics education. Designed as a qualitative case study, the research focused on seven teachers drawn from a broader maximum variation sample. Participants varied in years of teaching experience, graduate education, and self-reported AI experience. Data were collected through semi-structured online interviews and analyzed using descriptive content analysis focused on teachers’ pedagogical reasoning. Codes were developed from the teachers’ statements and organized into categories of pedagogical opportunities, pedagogical and epistemic risks, and conditions of use. The findings indicated that teachers did not reject AI categorically; rather, they viewed it as a complementary tool whose value depended on teacher guidance, the mathematical accuracy and conceptual appropriateness of generated content, and alignment with instructional purposes. Lesson planning, individualized feedback, visualization, and time efficiency were identified as the main opportunities. Concerns included inaccurate content entering teaching and assessment, misconceptions, overreliance on ready-made answers, and reduced student participation in learning. Controlled use and teacher oversight were recurring criteria across different experience profiles. The study clarifies the subject-specific criteria mathematics teachers use when judging whether AI use is pedagogically acceptable.
