Artificial intelligence in research is growing. Artificial intelligence brings chances to work faster but it also brings worries about whether legal sources are correct and trustworthy. These worries were highlighted in the case Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. In that case the Supreme Court of India looked at how the National Company Law Tribunal trusted artificial intelligence–generated legal material. The main dispute was about enforcing a guarantee but the Supreme Court's decision asked a bigger question: can a judge rely on legal references that do not exist? This paper looks at the facts of the case the Supreme Court's reasoning and what it means for lawyers, judges and the entire legal field. It shows the difference between using intelligence as a helper for research and treating artificial intelligence's unverified output as an official law source. The paper also talks about lawyers' duty to check citations and the need for courts and tribunals to check whether the authorities they see are real. Even though artificial intelligence helps with research the paper says that technology cannot replace careful work or judicial responsibility. The Supreme Court decision reminds us that every legal decision must depend on proven legal sources. The decision also raises questions about punishments and the safety measures needed as artificial intelligence becomes more common in law practice. In the end the paper says that technology can help with thinking but human professionals must keep the responsibility, for accuracy and integrity of legal work.

The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence in legal research has raised concerns about fabricated case law and the reliability of judicial decision making. In Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd., the Supreme Court of India examined the consequences of tribunals relying on non-existent and AI-hallucinated judicial precedents. The Court adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards unverified AI-generated authorities, set aside the orders of the NCLT and NCLAT, and directed the Bar Council of India to formulate guiding principles and disciplinary consequences. This case comment critically examines the judgment's implications for professional responsibility, judicial accountability and the legitimate use of artificial intelligence in adjudication. It evaluates the Court's strict approach, particularly its refusal to distinguish between material and incidental reliance on fabricated precedent, and identifies uncertainties concerning verification standards, judicial responsibility and the legal effect of tainted decisions. It argues that the judgment provides an important safeguard for the integrity of adjudication, but effective implementation requires clear, proportionate and enforceable standards for both the Bar and the Bench.

Abstract Copper nanoparticles (Cu NPs) have a broad applicability, yet their synthesis is sensitive to subtle changes in reaction parameters. This sensitivity, combined with the time- and resource-intensive nature of experimental optimization, poses a major challenge in achieving reproducible and size-controlled synthesis. While machine learning (ML) shows promise in materials research, its application is often limited by scarcity of large high-quality experimental data sets. This study explores ML to predict the DLS-derived hydrodynamic diameter of Cu NPs from microwave-assisted polyol synthesis using a small data set of 25 in-house performed syntheses. Latin hypercube sampling is used to efficiently cover the parameter space while creating the experimental data set. Ensemble regression models successfully predict hydrodynamic diameters with good predictive performance given the limited data set. Since quantitative regression requires a unique DLS-derived hydrodynamic diameter, the regression model is restricted to monomodal DLS distributions, while a complementary classification model identifies synthesis conditions for which quantitative prediction is applicable. Using equivalent out-of-sample validation (OOB and LOOCV), the ML and DoE models showed comparable generalization (MAE = 40.92 and 40.46 nm, respectively). The final ensemble model achieved an R2 of 0.74, an MAE of 23.81 nm, compared to an R2 of 0.60, an MAE of 33.54 nm for the DoE model, while retaining the complete synthesis parameter space, making it better suited for synthesis guidance. Additionally, classification models using both random forests and large language models (LLMs) are evaluated to distinguish between large and small particles. These classification models exhibited only modest predictive performance, indicating that this small data set is insufficient to fully exploit the capabilities of complex LLMs. Overall, this study demonstrates that carefully curated small data sets, paired with robust classical ML, can effectively support the synthesis of Cu NPs and highlights that for lab-scale studies, complex models like LLMs may offer limited benefits. The validation experiments further indicate the potential of ML guided synthesis to improve the efficiency of experimental optimization and reduce resource consumption.

Prefilled syringes (PFS) have undergone a paradigm shift, transitioning from passive primary container closure systems into complex, integrated drug-device combination products designed for modern biopharmaceuticals. Their ready-to-administer presentation streamlines clinical workflows, ensures rigorous dosing precision, minimizes contamination risks, and facilitates patient-centric home self-administration. The rapid proliferation of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins, peptides, and high concentration subcutaneous formulations has underscored the vital importance of container contact materials, silicone lubrication dynamics, needle geometry, and mechanical device integration. Contemporary PFS platforms encompass traditional Type I borosilicate glass, cyclic olefin polymer (COP), cyclic olefin copolymer (COC), and specialized silicone-reduced or silicone-free platforms. Each material matrix presents a distinct trade-off regarding gas/moisture barrier properties, fracture resistance, dimensional tolerances, extractables (E&L) profiles, and interface-induced drug degradation. For biological macromolecules, drug-container compatibility represents a critical quality attribute (CQA); protein adsorption and interfacial denaturation at glass, polymer, elastomer, air-liquid, and silicone-oil interfaces frequently induce subvisible particle generation and irreversible aggregation. Silicone oil microdroplets remain a focal technical challenge due to potential migration and nucleation effects, while residual manufacturing contaminants such as tungsten species can induce localized protein unfolding. Concurrently, injectability functionality is paramount for viscous high-concentration biologics, were hydraulic resistance and extrusion dynamics scale critically with needle lumen diameter and fluid rheology. This review provides a comprehensive review covering component architecture, material interaction pathways, silicone dynamics, fluid mechanical modelling, clinical human factors, regulatory frameworks, and next-generation smart delivery devices Keywords: Prefilled syringe; Drug-device combination system; Primary container closure; Biologics stability; Monoclonal antibodies; Silicone oil migration; Cyclic olefin polymer (COP); Injectability mechanics; Autoinjectors; Extractables and Leachables (E&L)

Introduction. Climate change has important implications for human health. Temperatures continue to rise and extreme weather conditions become more frequent. Resulting changes in ecosystems will impact health in general and more specifically, distribution of communicable, vector-borne and heat-related diseases. It is imperative to adopt proactive measures to anticipate and mitigate the health impact of climate change. New sensors, skills and tools are required to predict impact on human health and conceptualise proactive measures against adverse consequences of rising temperatures. Materials and methods. A search of the current literature on anticipatory research specific to sensors, skills and tools for prediction was employed. A design thinking model, the ClimateSense Model was conceptualised based on the analysis. Results. Sensors include physical sensors and information technology such as remote sensing with satellites, aircrafts and drones, biological sensors like RNA and DNA sequencing technologies, and chemical sensors for greenhouse gases. Tools include mobile applications and artificial intelligence, internet-of-things technology, and crowdsourcing. Skills involve digital skills to interpret and communicate sensor-derived data using interactive maps, plots, time series, and analysis of big data with statistical skills or artificial intelligence. Conclusion. Synergistic combination of tools, skills and sensors, as conceptualised in the ClimateSense model, are essential to anticipate consequences of climate change for health. By promoting anticipatory preparedness, policymakers, healthcare professionals and communities can better mitigate the adverse health impacts of climate change, build resilience to its effects and define a planetary health strategy. Key messages. Climate change significantly impacts human health through rising temperatures and ecosystem changes. New sensors, tools, and skills are essential to predict and mitigate health consequences of climate change. The ClimateSense model promotes proactive strategies to enhance preparedness and resilience against climate-related health risks.

Background: Due to prolonged slouching and biomechanical overload from feeding, this becomes common among breastfeeding moms. This posture can bring about scapular dyskinesis like the SICK scapular syndrome.Objective: To determine the prevalence and patterns of shoulder pain and functional disability associated with scapular dyskinesis among lactating mothers.Methods:A cross sectional observational study of 100 lactating mothers in the age group of 20-40 years was conducted to assess shoulder pain and disability by pain scoring using visual analogue scale (VAS), disability scoring by shoulder pain and disability index (SPADI), and to screen for scapular dyskinesia using lateral scapular slide test (LSST). Statistical analysis was done using SPSS software 25.0.Result: Most participants reported Bilateral (68%) symptoms compared to the unilateral scapular Involvement (32%) mainly involving dominant side. According to SPADI 37% had moderate pain, 5% had light pain, and 58% had severe pain. The most problematic functional limitations were those which involve pushing the affected limb (47% moderate, 21% severe), to reach for something (48% moderate, 24% severe) and to carry anything (67% had considerable problems). Only those concerning the wearing of shirts and pants where more than 75% of mothers had only few problems. A statistically significant positive association was found between the duration of lactation and the age of the mothers (r=0.567; p<0.01) with greater pain to the shoulders.Conclusion: Early ergonomic support and physiotherapy might have a key role in symptoms management and to reduce further long-term problems of musculoskeletal nature. The results indicate a significant presence of SICK scapular Syndrome and Shoulder pain in lactating Mothers particularly among those having prolonged periods of Breast feeding.

This protocol describes a scoping review that will identify, map, and synthesize the outcomes and measurement tools used in empirical research on manuscript peer review, providing the initial evidence base for the Primary Evaluation outcomEs for Research on peer review - A Core Outcome Set (PEER-COS). Guided by JBI methodology and the COMET Handbook and COS-STAD principles, the review will search seven bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and 69 grey-literature sources for eligible English-language systematic reviews, experimental, quasi-experimental, and observational studies published from 1986 onwards. Eligible studies must evaluate an empirically measured outcome related to peer review of scholarly manuscripts, including, for example, quality, timeliness, transparency, fairness, reliability, or stakeholder experience. Screening and data extraction will be supported by the otto-SR artificial-intelligence platform and subject to predefined human quality checks; identified outcomes will be synthesized quantitatively and thematically into unique outcome concepts and broader domains. The resulting candidate outcome list will inform a three-round international Delphi consensus process involving relevant interest holders—including researchers, editors, peer reviewers, funders, statisticians, and patient and public partners—to establish a core outcome set for future research evaluating manuscript peer review and peer-review interventions.

The article is devoted to the problem of detecting faulty conditions and cases of improper maintenance of automatic fire detection and public alert systems. The aim of the work is to systematize the causes of failures and false alarms, as well as to analyze the regulatory legal risk indicators that allow supervisory authorities to identify potentially hazardous facilities. The study provides a detailed classification of the causes of false alarms, distinguishing four key groups: technical malfunctions, violations of operating conditions, environmental influences and the human factor. The risk indicators approved by Order of EMERCOM of Russia № 364 are analyzed, and the impact of electrical faults (overload, short circuit, high contact resistance) on the operability of system components is considered. Based on the provisions of GOST R 59638-2021 and GOST R 59639-2021, practical recommendations are formulated for ensuring operational reliability at the stages of design, commissioning and maintenance. The novelty of the work lies in the comprehensive linking of the risk indicators used by supervisory authorities with specific physical equipment defects and organizational maintenance errors.

In unavoidable crash scenarios, vehicles may have to allocate harm between occupants and pedestrians, raising a central question for autonomous vehicle ethics: should they prioritize occupant protection or minimize overall casualties? This study examines public acceptance of casualty-minimizing stay and occupant-protective swerve maneuvers in moral dilemmas involving human-driven vehicles (HDVs) and autonomous vehicles (AVs), with one occupant and one to five pedestrians. Based on data from Chinese participants (N = 1,188), the results show that participants generally accepted occupant sacrifice when it spared multiple pedestrians, and that acceptance of casualty minimization increased as pedestrian numbers increased. However, the same stay maneuver received lower acceptance when performed by an AV than by an HDV, especially in the one-occupant-versus-one-pedestrian scenario. These findings extend AV ethics research beyond forced-choice preferences by showing how people evaluate concrete vehicle maneuvers, and offer empirical evidence for designing and governing ethical decision rules in unavoidable crash scenarios.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Abstract Accurate quantitative mapping of gamma-ray emitters is critical for applications ranging from radiological emergency response and environmental monitoring to nuclear security and deep space exploration. Here, we show that such mapping can be achieved by combining mobile gamma-ray spectrometry with high-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations and full-spectrum Bayesian inference. Using 6 s of single-pass mobile spectrometry data benchmarked against independent in-situ and laboratory assays, we demonstrate decisive source mixture identification (>5 σ ), meter-scale source localization, and recovery of source activities with percent-level accuracy. The developed method marks a critical advance in quantitative gamma-ray sensing, enabling improved radiological situational awareness, enhanced terrestrial geophysical and geochemical mapping, as well as more robust constraints on radionuclide abundances on extraterrestrial bodies across the Solar System.

Background and Aims Patient education materials (PEMs) support patient understanding and engagement in care. This study evaluated the readability, understandability and actionability of non-oncological urological PEMs produced by the British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) and the European Association of Urology (EAU), and explored agreement between human and AI-assisted PEMAT-P assessment. Methods and Results A cross-sectional descriptive analysis assessed eight matched PEMs relating to urinary tract infection, urinary incontinence, benign prostatic enlargement/lower urinary tract symptoms, and nocturnal polyuria. Readability was assessed using Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG), and Gunning Fog Index. Understandability and actionability were assessed using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT-P). Mean FKGL was 11.85 ± 2.77, SMOG 13.24 ± 2.39, Gunning Fog 14.09 ± 3.22, and FRE 48.5 ± 13.32. All materials exceeded the recommended reading level. Mean PEMAT-P understandability and actionability were 91.0% and 88.3%. Human–AI item-level agreement for understandability and actionability was 83.6% and 81.8%; Cohen's κ was 0.25 and 0.23, and Gwet's AC1 was 0.79 and 0.76. Conclusion The materials exceeded recommended reading levels despite variable PEMAT-P scores. Human vs AI differences remained, requiring further evaluation of PEMs to establish the potential role of AI as an adjunct to human PEMAT-P assessment.

This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence aligns with human experts in the visual assessment of urban open spaces. Site quality is addressed across five dimensions: spatial accessibility and organization; usage and social function; environmental quality and comfort; safety and inclusivity; and perceptual and aesthetic quality. The same images, indicators, and five-point scale regarding three heavily used public open spaces in Rize city center were evaluated by 20 architects and landscape architects, as well as by ChatGPT and Gemini. The comparison revealed that the level of agreement between the AI and the experts varied depending on the specific site and quality dimension. While alignment was high regarding features that are directly observable—both physically and visually—differences became more pronounced regarding perceptual and aesthetic qualities. The findings suggest that AI can serve as a complementary tool to support visual assessment rather than a replacement for human expertise.

Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition (HGR) has emerged as a key model of modern Human Computer Interaction (HCI) technologies, enabling touchless and intuitive interactive experiences for a wide range of HCI applications, from assistive technology, virtual and augmented reality to industrial production lines. Although AI and DL open up important opportunities, there are practical challenges to developing and deploying real-time HGR systems that are strong to issues such as computational complexity, variations in the environment, and latency. This survey reviews the state-of-the-art in real-time HGR, including recent work in and algorithmic approaches for various sensor modalities and different stages of the processing pipeline, including detection, tracking, and spatial-temporal classification, using monocular RGB cameras and multi-modal depth sensing systems. In addition, we cover applications such as sign language recognition, healthcare hygiene systems, automotive user interfaces, and human-robot collaboration (HRC), and challenges such as occlusion invariance, light variability, performance versus portability trade-offs, constraints imposed by edge-device deployment, and potential research avenues for multimodal artificial intelligence systems of the future.

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Advances in multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis and treatment have altered disease trajectories, yet many people with MS (pwMS) continue to experience complex symptom burden, functional limitations, and reduced quality of life (QoL). This review summarizes recent developments in neurorehabilitation, focusing on screening and assessment, intervention delivery, and outcome or impact evaluation across symptoms and disability domains. RECENT FINDINGS: Research evidence supports routine, multidimensional screening that goes beyond assessing symptom severity to capture functional limitations, participation restrictions, and social determinants of health (SDoH). Digital technologies, including wearables, remote monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted assessments, offer opportunities for more ecologically valid and accessible evaluation, although usability, digital exclusion, and implementation issues remain. Neurorehabilitation is increasingly viewed as a treatment that should begin early in the disease course rather than being reserved for advanced disability. Exercise interventions, cognitive rehabilitation, psychological therapies, vocational rehabilitation, and integrated multidisciplinary approaches demonstrate benefits across physical, cognitive, emotional, fatigue, and QoL outcomes. Telerehabilitation and technology-supported interventions, including virtual reality, exergaming, and neuromodulation, show promise in improving access and outcomes, but more research is needed. To sustain long-term neurorehabilitation benefits, teaching self-management strategies and brain-health behaviours may be beneficial. SUMMARY: Neurorehabilitation is a core component of comprehensive MS care, complementing pharmacological treatment. Evidence favours early, personalized, function-focused interventions delivered through flexible, tiered, and multidisciplinary models. Research gaps include implementation of screening pathways, optimization of person-to-treatment matching and dosing, integration of SDoH, development of meaningful patient-centred outcomes, evaluation of cost-effectiveness, and improved equity of access to rehabilitation services and research across diverse populations.

Abstract Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous breast cancer subtype for which artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment response applications. This study presents a comparative bibliometric analysis of AI-related TNBC research indexed in Scopus (n=1,037), Web of Science (n=557), and PubMed (n=763) from 2013-2026. Publication trends, citation impact, leading contributors, international collaboration, knowledge structure, and thematic evolution were examined using database-appropriate bibliometric and network analyses. Using complete year data through 2025, publication output showed statistically significant increasing trends across all three databases, with 2020-2025 compound annual growth rates of 50.13% for Scopus, 49.78% for Web of Science, and 42.84% for PubMed. The United States emerged as the dominant international collaboration hub, while collaboration between the United States and China formed the strongest bilateral link. Thematic evolution showed an early emphasis on machine learning, followed by expansion of deep learning and radiomics and, more recently, parallel imaging/computational and clinical/biological themes involving MRI, treatment response prediction, the tumor microenvironment, immunotherapy, and precision medicine. Scopus co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses further identified established intellectual foundations and contemporary research fronts. Overall, AI-TNBC research is expanding rapidly, while data heterogeneity, external validation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain important challenges.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence in primary education is changing the way teaching materials are structured, information is acquired, and learning decisions are made. These changes require a reconsideration of the teacher's position, particularly when system recommendations begin to influence assessments of children's needs and abilities. This article aims to redefine the role of primary school teachers through the relationship between pedagogical agency, knowledge authority, and educational ethics. The review employs a critical narrative literature approach to 19 selected publications from 2021–2026, encompassing empirical research, research reviews, conceptual articles, and policy documents that provide open access or official download facilities. The literature is reviewed based on educational context, type of evidence, conceptual contributions, and limitations of its application to primary schools. The synthesis shows that the benefits of AI depend on learning objectives, professional judgment capacity, and institutional support. Teacher agency requires the authority to review, modify, and reject system recommendations. Knowledge authority rests on the ability to explain the basis for a claim and guide the examination of evidence. Educational ethics need to be embodied in data protection, equitable access, child engagement, and the sharing of responsibilities. The article proposes the role of teachers as learning designers, knowledge assessors, relational facilitators, and advocates for children's interests. This reconceptualization requires case-based professional development and school governance that does not center all technological risks on teachers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Aeon Mundi is a collection of adaptive furnishings and robotic tools designed to connect small-plot, rotational food growing with the everyday life of homes, civic buildings, and shared public spaces. Its six pieces support a connected journey from cultivation and habitat care to harvesting, processing, and transport. Workstations, companion seating, and autonomous carts combine adjustable ergonomics with robotic assistance for moving crops, trays, and tools, keeping people involved at each stage. A common material language unites the collection: polished solid-cast mycelium in natural, vegetable-pigmented hues; sustainably loomed bamboo upholstery; rounded, repairable forms; and fine luminescent accents that respond to work phases. Embedded spatial displays offer abstract, user-invoked cues. Together, these elements frame food production as an accessible part of shared daily life and propose a design system for exploring how productive landscapes and human-centered technology can coexist.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

Governments are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver services, process cases and inform policy, but the success of these initiatives depends less on the technology than on the capabilities of the public workforce that must use, oversee and explain it. Evidence on how AI reshapes tasks suggests that routine cognitive work is most exposed, while demand grows for analytical, interpersonal and ethical judgement. Yet research on public-sector AI has concentrated on technology adoption and governance, and far less on the reskilling and leadership needed to make adoption work. This paper addresses that gap through an integrative review of literature from public administration, labour economics, leadership and learning science, supplemented by policy sources. The review identifies three capability clusters that AI-enabled public administration requires: digital-technical capability, human-relational capability and adaptive leadership capability. It also finds that evidence-based learning designs, particularly spaced, retrieval-based microlearning embedded in work, offer a scalable route to building these capabilities across large civil services. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and transformational leadership theory, the paper proposes the AI-Ready Public Workforce Capability Framework, which links institutional enablers, capability clusters and learning architecture to public value outcomes. Four propositions and practical recommendations are offered for public managers and training institutions, with reference to India’s Mission Karmayogi.

Organisations adopting artificial intelligence must reskill large parts of their workforce, and the success of reskilling is usually measured by course completion, which says little about whether employees can actually work with AI tools. This paper examines whether learning analytics, the behavioural traces of how employees engage with reskilling, can predict workforce readiness, defined as demonstrated capability to use AI in the job, and how readiness predictions should direct support. A simulation of 3,000 employees generates readiness from a process in which practice, completion, assessment, peer interaction, prior digital skill and recency all contribute, with practice and completion interacting. A gradient-boosting model on the full set of learning-analytics features attains an AUC of 0.75, against 0.68 for completion and assessment scores alone. Practice sessions (0.09) and module completion (0.08) are the strongest predictors, with assessment scores (0.04) and prior digital skill (0.04) secondary. A targeting simulation shows that directing a fixed support budget to employees with marginal predicted readiness raises overall readiness by 4.5 points, against 3.1 points for random allocation. The paper argues that reskilling should be managed on practice and application rather than completion, that readiness predictions should direct support toward employees near the threshold, and that learning analytics should be governed as employee data with developmental purpose.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: The use of biomass fuel in households has many adverse health effects and the use of such fuel in cooking environments as an occupational exposure setting remain unexplored. This study aims to examine the extent of respiratory health risks, as a consequence of exposure to biomass fuel smoke, of cook-cum-helpers of the Mid-Day Meal scheme in rural Assam, India. We utilized a comparative cross sectional study design to investigate 130 cook-cum-helpers from 28 government schools (65 from firewood kitchens and 65 from LPG kitchens). The respiratory symptoms of participants were documented using the standard American Thoracic Society (ATS) questionnaire and pulmonary function tests were conducted using spirometry. Based on the confounders of household biomass exposure and passive smoking, propensity score matching was employed. The Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATET) approach was used and matched regression models were computed in the presence of cluster standard school level errors. The mixed effects and cluster adjusted models were used to conduct sensitivity analyses. Of the matched study population ( n = 116) firewood exposure was found to increase the probability of reporting at least one respiratory symptom by 28.4% points (95% CI 15.6–41.2) and airway obstruction by 22.1% points (95% CI 8.4–35.8). Those firewood exposed workers experienced a 13.95% point greater decline in the mean FEV₁ percent-predicted. A significant exposure–duration gradient (p-trend < 0.001) was found that supports the increase in respiratory health risks with longer durations of employment. These findings were valid across different specifications. Institutional school kitchens that utilize biomass fuel are an occupational health hazard that has and continues to remain underestimated. These findings underscore the need to improve occupational health policies and accelerate the use of clean cooking fuels. However, the cross-sectional design of the study limits causal analysis.

INTRODUCTION: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools become increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding how engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity and responsible AI use has become increasingly important. OBJECTIVES: This study investigates how master’s engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity, and responsible AI use. It also explores the potential relevance of these practices for the development of competencies associated with participation in data-driven and AI-enabled professional environments. METHODS: A mixed-methods approach was employed using the PEDRA questionnaire (Perceptions on Ethics and Development of Responsibility in Academia), developed by the authors. The instrument was designed to explore students’ perceptions, experiences, and ethical reasoning regarding academic integrity and responsible research practices. The analysis focused on two questionnaire items addressing the influence of academic honesty on data use and the frequency of AI tool use in academic activities. The study involved master’s engineering students from two higher education institutions. RESULTS: Based on the 48 complete responses analysed, the findings indicate awareness of data integrity principles, particularly regarding anonymity, confidentiality, informed consent, and rigorous data analysis. Ethical referencing and transparency in data handling were mentioned less frequently, suggesting areas for further educational support. Regarding AI adoption, 21 of 48 respondents (43.8%) reported occasional use of AI tools, reflecting a cautious and exploratory approach. Descriptive differences in AI use were observed across age and gender groups, with female respondents being more likely to explore AI while maintaining ethical awareness, although these findings should be interpreted with caution. CONCLUSION: The study highlights the importance of integrating responsible data and AI practices into engineering education. The results suggest that developing students’ capacity to use data and AI critically, transparently, and ethically may support the development of competencies associated with responsible participation in increasingly digital and AI-enabled environments. The PEDRA questionnaire demonstrates potential as an exploratory and diagnostic instrument for identifying educational needs related to academic integrity, responsible AI use, data integrity, and trustworthy digital practice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into educational feedback offers opportunities to expand personalisation and accessibility, but it also raises risks of bias, opacity and the erosion of teacher mediation. The objective of this theoretical-conceptual article was to propose a framework to guide the use of generative AI in feedback from the standpoint of inclusive assessment and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). As method, a selective narrative review of the literature on inclusive assessment, formative feedback and AI in education was conducted across three strands, which were then integrated into a framework of teacher decisions and transversal criteria, contrasted with related models and complemented by a focused search of recent studies on trust and evaluative judgement. As a result, the framework links four teacher decisions (what is assessed, how evidence is gathered, how feedback is given, and what opportunities for improvement are offered) with three transversal quality criteria: accessibility, agency and dialogue, and equity with data protection. It is complemented by a four-level scale of teacher mediation that distinguishes lower- and higher-risk uses, a checklist for reviewing AI-supported feedback before it reaches students, three illustrative examples, and five testable propositions to guide empirical validation. The implications of the framework for teaching practice and institutional policy are discussed, along with its tensions (efficiency versus dialogicity, personalisation versus privacy, linguistic diversity, and the access gap) and its methodological limitations. The article concludes that inclusion does not depend on the tool but on the pedagogical and ethical decisions that govern its use, and that teacher responsibility for interpreting evidence remains irreplaceable.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Understanding drivers’ visual attention adaptation under dynamic lane change risk supports human-centric interaction design. We synchronized eye-tracking metrics, vehicle motion logs, and front-view videos from 36 professional drivers in a naturalistic field experiment. A computer vision-based framework was proposed to extract surrounding vehicle kinematics from monocular footage, and a Modified Lane Change Risk Index was developed to quantify dynamic risk. Results reveal directional heterogeneity, with right lane changes involving conservative scanning and significantly prolonged fixations on the initial lane compared with leftward maneuvers. As risk escalated, drivers prioritized safety-critical areas, with increased saccade frequency and shortened fixation durations. In high-risk right lane changes, the Near Lane Line served as a visual anchor for trajectory correction. High-risk states persisted from execution into stabilization, while drivers tended to lock their gaze on the target lane and neglect side mirror checks. These findings inform risk-adaptive human-machine interfaces and human-centric co-driving systems.

Study Protocol This study protocol presents a reproducible framework for a retrospective secondary analysis of real-world hospital encounters involving patients with diabetes. The proposed research uses the publicly available Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, containing 101,766 historical hospital encounters recorded between 1999 and 2008. The study aims to develop and evaluate a risk-stratified prioritization approach for potential patient follow-up under hypothetical healthcare service-capacity constraints. The planned methodology includes data preprocessing, prediction of observed 30-day hospital readmission, comparison of prioritization strategies, and exploratory assessment of equity-related performance. Research status: This document is a study protocol. Empirical analysis of the original dataset has not yet been completed or independently validated. No observed effects of war, crisis-related service disruption, or clinical interventions are claimed. Capacity-constrained scenarios are hypothetical. Data source: UCI Machine Learning Repository. DOI: 10.24432/C5230J. Transparency statement: OpenAI ChatGPT assisted with initial document structuring and analytical code drafting. The author is responsible for reviewing, validating, and verifying the research before publication. Peer-review status: Not peer reviewed. Author: Elnaz Abedini, Doctoral Student in Biomedical Engineering, Karabük University, Türkiye.

This chapter examines the critical role of communities of practice in developing technology leadership capabilities within higher education. Drawing from participant interviews, institutional case studies, and the authors’ direct experiences, we analyze how formal and informal communities shape professional development and organizational innovation. We present detailed examples of successful communities of practice ranging from institutional programs like Dartmouth LEADS and Harvard’s ABCD Committee to cross-institutional collaboratives including the Ivy+ Classroom and Learning Space Technologies (CLST) group and the HAIL Storm network. Our analysis reveals that effective communities of practice share three essential elements: a clearly defined domain of knowledge, an established community of engaged participants, and commitment to evolving shared practices. Key success factors include appropriate group size balancing intimacy with inclusivity, sustainable leadership structures, institutional support for participation, and adaptable meeting formats. The research demonstrates that communities of practice provide critical benefits including peer learning opportunities, professional network development, benchmarking capabilities, and collaborative problem-solving resources – particularly valuable during periods of technological disruption like the emergence of generative AI. For technology leaders, strategic engagement with communities of practice offers pathways for personal development, team enhancement, and organizational advancement. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations for identifying, participating in, and fostering communities of practice as essential leadership development tools in rapidly evolving technological landscapes.

AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. We conclude with actionable implications emphasizing mitigations beyond model-level safeguards such as content filtering: age assurance, consent verification for depiction, safety-by-design UX constraints, incident disclosure norms, and auditing regimes targeting developmental risk. Privacy-minimized annotations, a codebook, and documentation are available at https://github.com/The-Responsible-AI-Initiative/KidAID.

Abstract Accurately predicting protein stability changes upon residue-level mutations is essential for protein engineering and design. However, previous computational methods are typically designed for specific tasks and struggle to generalize across different stability systems, preventing the accurate guidance of protein mutagenesis. Sequence-based methods are easier to apply to large-scale protein datasets since they do not rely on high-quality structures. However, existing sequence-based approaches struggle to capture structural changes, resulting in lower performance compared to structure-based methods. In this study, we pro-pose DeepTherm, a sequence-based deep learning solution to model changes in folding free energy (∆∆G) and melting temperature (∆Tm) resulting from single-point mutations. DeepTherm transfers a protein large language model as a core component and incorporates a cross-attention mechanism to capture the contact-map changes around mutated positions. To address data imbalance and the antisymmetric nature of mutation effects, DeepTherm employs a self-distillation inference strategy under the supervision of an antisymmetric constraint. Benchmarking across multiple datasets shows that DeepTherm achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in both ∆∆G and ∆Tm predictions. Furthermore, practical evaluations confirm DeepTherm's capability in accurately ranking protein stability on large-scale datasets and effectively identifying critical structural contacts impacting stability. Detailed analysis on cDNA display proteolysis data further highlights the critical importance of self-distillation and antisymmetric constraints in enhancing predictive performance.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education to support experiential learning in customer service training, where applying theoretical frameworks such as the SERVQUAL model can be challenging. Students frequently struggle with emotional recognition, immediate decision-making, and applying SERVQUAL dimensions during role-play. To address these gaps, this study introduces ServeSmart, an AI-supported learning system that provides real-time guidance during customer service scenario role-play. Using a preliminary exploratory quantitative survey design, this study evaluated students' perceived learning experiences and the platform's usability. Using a non-probability purposive sampling strategy, 30 undergraduate students participated in individual scenario-based simulations followed by a validated post-evaluation questionnaire. Baseline findings indicated that a majority of participants had difficulty with emotional recognition and lacked immediate instructional feedback during simulations. Post-simulation results revealed that all participants reported higher perceived confidence in executing customer service tasks, a clearer perceived understanding of SERVQUAL concepts, and strong interest in future platform utilization. Overall, the findings demonstrate positive student perceptions of ServeSmart as a supportive experiential learning tool, highlighting its potential to offer an immediate instructional platform in service management education.

Petroleum stations, also known as filling stations or gas stations, primarily distribute diesel fuel and gasoline to motor vehicles while simultaneously releasing gases and vapours that contribute to various forms of environmental pollution. This study investigated sex-based variations in blood parameters among forecourt attendants in Port Harcourt, Nigeria. This research was structured as a comparative cross-sectional study utilising randomised sampling techniques. A total of 100 participants, including 50 fuel station workers and 50 non-fuel station workers as controls, were enrolled. Key parameters such as white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration and biochemical markers were analysed to assess the impact of occupational exposure to petroleum vapours. The data collected in this study were expressed as Mean ± Standard Deviation and analysed using SPSS version 23. Results indicated that while most haematological parameters showed no significant gender differences, females exhibited notably lower haemoglobin (p= <0.0001) and packed cell volume (p= 0.001) compared to males, suggesting a higher vulnerability to the hematotoxic effects of fuel exposure. Additionally, significant deviations in absolute lymphocyte counts (p= 0.024) were observed, indicating potential immunological implications for female workers. The findings underscore the necessity for targeted health interventions and regular monitoring to mitigate health risks associated with prolonged exposure to petroleum products. It is crucial to implement preventive measures, including regular health screenings, nutritional support and improved workplace safety protocols. These interventions will be essential in safeguarding the health of fuel station workers and addressing the occupational health disparities identified in this study.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The most common and fatal type of cancer worldwide is skin cancer. Prompt treatment and improved patient results rely on the prompt finding and accurate labeling of skin lesions. As deep learning and artificial intelligence progress, automated diagnostic systems have demonstrated encouraging outcomes, especially when developed using extensive dermatological images. This chapter proposed CNN architecture for skin lesions classification utilizing the HAM10000 (“Human Against Machine with 10000 training images”) dataset. 10,015 dermatoscopic pictures collected from diverse demographics and imaging modalities are included in the HAM10000 collection. It includes seven clinically important categories of pigmented skin lesions: Melanocytic nevi (nv): harmless mole-like growths, Melanoma (mel): a severe and aggressive type of skin cancer, Benign keratosis-like lesions (bkl): which comprise seborrheic keratoses and solar lentigines, The most common types of skin cancer are basal cell carcinoma (bcc), actinic keratoses, and intraepithelial carcinoma (akiec): pre-cancerous and early-stage cancerous lesions, Vascular lesions (vasc): which encompass angiomas and haemorrhages, and Dermatofibroma (df): non-cancerous skin nodules. To enhance model performance and ensure data quality, preprocessing methods like Gaussian filtering followed by Grab-Cut segmentation to extract affected area, and data augmentation are utilized for class imbalance issue. The Proposed CNN used to extract the feature; finally soft max classifier is used to classify 7 types of skin disease with validation accuracy of 98.67. This chapter also highlight various CNN Architecture and discuss challenges in recent skin disease classification.

topics: Effects of Environmental Stressors on Livestock

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming paediatric dentistry by supporting dentists in diagnosis, treatment planning, behaviour management, and patient education. AI-based technologies such as machine learning and deep learning enable accurate interpretation of dental images, early detection of caries, prediction of eruption patterns, and identification of developmental anomalies. In addition, AI powered mobile applications, virtual assistants, and chatbots improve communication, reduce dental anxiety, and enhance oral health education among children and parents. These digital tools help personalise care while reducing clinical workload and improving efficiency. This review highlights the evolution of AI in paediatric dentistry, its key applications across behavioural management, diagnostics, forensic identification, and patient communication, as well as its benefits, challenges, and future potential in improving child centred dental care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cybersecurity is increasingly recognised as a complex adaptive socio-technical system in which security outcomes emerge from the interactions of attackers, defenders, users, organisations, regulators, and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents. These interactions generate adaptive feedback loops, strategic behaviour, information diffusion, and network effects that drive the evolution of cyber threats and defences. Consequently, phenomena such as attack propagation, cyber-risk contagion, cascading failures, and systemic resilience cannot be fully understood through static or purely technical perspectives. Although evolutionary game theory (EGT), complex systems science, network science, behavioural research, and cyber economics have each provided valuable insights, the literature remains fragmented, with no unified perspective for explaining cybersecurity as an evolving socio-technical ecosystem. This review develops the concept of Social Physics of Cybersecurity as an interdisciplinary perspective that brings these approaches together with human-AI interaction to explain how collective security outcomes emerge from adaptive interactions within interconnected cyber ecosystems. We synthesise research on attacker-defender co-evolution, finite and structured population dynamics, cyber contagion, critical transitions, systemic cyber risk, and the growing role of AI-enabled multi-agent systems. Building on these perspectives, we propose a unified multilevel view of cybersecurity that links individual strategic behaviour, network-level interactions, and system-wide resilience. We argue that cybersecurity should be understood as a social-physical phenomenon in which resilience and vulnerability emerge from the collective dynamics of interacting human and artificial agents. Finally, we identify key research opportunities for developing empirically grounded, data-driven, and AI-enabled models capable of predicting, analysing, and governing increasingly interconnected and autonomous cyber ecosystems.

Individuals with intellectual disabilities face entrenched systemic and cultural barriers to sexual expression, often exacerbated in Chinese contexts by values of ‘face’ and ‘familism’. While artificial intelligence and humanoid sex robots emerge as potential interventions, their ethical and practical viability within disability services remains contested. This study employed Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the perspectives of 12 Chinese social workers regarding the integration of AI-powered intimate technologies. Findings reveal four major themes: systemic barriers to romantic agency, the perceived benefits of ‘risk-free’ simulated intimacy, ethical concerns regarding relational authenticity, and societal reflections on the ‘eternal child’ syndrome. Practitioners recognised robots as tools to bypass parental opposition and institutional liability by eliminating risks of pregnancy and exploitation. However, a critical tension emerged: whether these technologies genuinely empower users or serve as a ‘techno-fix’ to hide disabled sexuality from the neurotypical public. The results highlight a ‘double standard of readiness’, where cognitive competence is used to gatekeep human rights. We argue for a multidisciplinary governance framework that prioritises ‘techno-social’ literacy and challenges the sexual ableism inherent in current service models.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

Sovereign artificial intelligence has moved from a legal debate about data residency to a practical question of agency across the whole computational value chain: energy, connectivity, data centres, compute, data, models, applications, skills and governance. This paper reviews an AI-generated report that models national compute ecosystems through infrastructure economics, low-precision arithmetic, game theory and Monte Carlo risk analysis, and augments it into a verified academic treatment. Each empirical claim in the source was checked against institutional sources. Several were confirmed: the scale of the CNAS Sovereign AI Index, the UK Council for Science and Technology's definition of sovereignty as agency, the European AI Gigafactories call and its deadline changes, Bangladesh's draft National AI Policy 2026–2030, the OECD's 2026 due diligence guidance and the specifications of current rack-scale systems. Others were corrected, notably the infrastructure share of projects and the temporary nature of a mid-2026 suspension of foreign access to frontier models; unverifiable figures were removed. The augmentation adds three computed analyses. A synthetic quantisation experiment shows why block-scaled 4-bit formats are central to doing more with scarce national compute. A corrected analysis of the source's openness model shows that its optimum is a single planner's choice, not a Nash equilibrium, and derives its comparative statics. A Monte Carlo schedule model shows that headline probabilities of infrastructure delay depend entirely on assumed distributions and should be reported with them. The paper closes with implications for capital-constrained states, with Bangladesh as a reference case, framed at the level of strategy and policy.

Many institutions have come to recognize the importance of designing physical and digital learning environments based on what we know about how students learn. While higher education can support active learning anywhere, choice architecture suggests that where we learn has a significant impact on how we learn. This chapter will focus on a 25-year retrospective case analysis of leading change with developing physical and digital learning environments at a research-intensive university, through multiple educational disruptions. Adaptations to these changes are structured using change frameworks from the literature to distill four key areas. First, “developing a collaborative vision, governance, and strategic planning” moved opportunistic events to a structured vision. “Decisions based on pedagogical principles, diversity and inclusion” focused on student success and what research has demonstrated can enable successful learning to guide decisions. “Create comprehensive sustainable support” enables a shift of thinking on emerging technologies to look at pedagogical innovation for the long term. Lastly, a “focus on data driven decision making” avoids anecdotal change to support decisions based on actual evidence. This chapter will look toward the future and how learning environments continue to contribute to future teaching and learning success as we adapt to a new disruption bringing us into the age of artificial intelligence (AI). We conclude with recommendations for leaders and centers for teaching and learning (CTLs) on planning physical and digital learning environments and preparing for the next wave of disruption.

Objective To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education. Methods A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing. Results The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R 2 = 0.333, adjusted R 2 = 0.311, F = 15.030, P < 0.001) Conclusion Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Discipline in memorizing the Qur’an is an important aspect of the tahfiz program because students are required to be consistent in memorizing, reviewing, and maintaining their memorization. In its implementation, students have different levels of motivation, memorization ability, and readiness to submit their memorization. Some students are still reluctant to submit their memorization, lack focus during learning activities, or experience difficulties in maintaining consistency. Therefore, teacher strategies are needed to support students in developing discipline in memorizing the Qur’an. This study aims to describe the strategies applied by teachers to improve discipline in Qur’an memorization among eighth-grade students in the tahfiz program at MTs Assa’adah II Bungah Gresik, the impact of these strategies, and the supporting and inhibiting factors in their implementation. This research employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. The data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles and Huberman through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that teachers applied strategies including setting memorization targets according to students’ abilities, habituating muroja’ah, providing examples, and giving motivation and guidance to students. The strategies had an impact on students’ discipline in maintaining memorization, conducting muroja’ah, managing their time, and achieving memorization targets. Supporting factors included a conducive learning environment, students’ intrinsic motivation, parental support, and teacher guidance and motivation. Inhibiting factors included fluctuating student motivation, differences in memorization abilities, lack of readiness for memorization submission, and distractions during learning activities. These findings indicate that teacher strategies play a role in supporting the development of students’ discipline and consistency in Qur’an memorization.

Language education, particularly English for Academic/Specific Purposes (EAP/ESP), is navigating a period of systemic disruption. The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence, arriving just after the significant upheaval of the COVID-19 pandemic, has once again altered institutional policies and reshaped student needs. This continuous flux leaves many practitioners in a state of constant reactivity. In line with the conference theme, Innovations in Language Education: Advancing Pedagogy, Practice and Research, we argue for a shift away from responding to educational change toward anticipating and influencing it. This paper presents the conceptual framework and insights gleaned from participants in a Futures Workshop conducted at the conference. Drawing on the multidisciplinary field of Futures Studies (FS), the workshop introduced language educators to three foundational foresight methodologies: Metaphors, the Futures Triangle, and Scenario Planning. Contextualised within the English as a Medium of Instruction environment of Hong Kong, the paper outlines the theoretical rationale for applying FS to strategic thinking within language education, details the workshop's design, and presents initial participant perspectives on the field's trajectory. We conclude that equipping educators with Futures Literacy is critical for cultivating teacher agency, enabling us to design and advocate for preferable pedagogical futures.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support independent preparation without necessarily strengthening students’ connections to the classroom. We examined a structured instructional protocol combining AI exploration, confidence reflection, unresolved question generation, and instructor responsiveness. Following baseline assessment, six intact undergraduate class sections at one Chinese university were randomized equally, with three sections and 110 students assigned to each condition. Assessments were conducted in Weeks 1, 6, and 12, and the intervention began in Week 2. Recomputed item means were analyzed using equally weighted section-level contrasts with four degrees of freedom, supplemented by exact randomization tests. At Week 12, the between-condition difference in classroom belonging change was 0.361 (95% CI 0.145 to 0.576; Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.029). The corresponding differences were 0.282 for emotional engagement, − 0.497 for reactance to teacher guidance, and − 15.24 points for the confidence–performance discrepancy index (CPDI). Exact two-sided randomization p values were 0.100 for all primary contrasts, the minimum attainable with six balanced sections. Exploratory individual-level pathway and effect-modification analyses were treated as hypothesis-generating because only six sections were observed and the pathway estimates were sensitive to measurement timing. Overall, the structured protocol showed promising differences in classroom belonging and related outcomes, but inference remains limited by the small number of randomized sections, parametric model assumptions, and the preliminary discrepancy measure. The findings therefore concern the combined instructional protocol rather than an isolated effect of GenAI or an established psychological mechanism.

Abstract Graduate employability programmes are usually evaluated with self-report measures. We compared a structured human resource development programme supported by generative AI with career guidance matched on topics, duration and facilitator contact. Twelve intact cohorts of graduates seeking education-sector posts in Guangdong, China (N = 186), were allocated as whole units, six per condition, crossed with institution, facilitator and schedule. Blinded experts gave a global rating (0–100) of recruitment-task materials produced on site, under invigilation and without AI, before and after the programme. Ratings were made without a pre-specified rubric, which limits their interpretation. Among 168 participants with post-test data (overall attrition 9.7%), the adjusted difference favoured the AI-supported programme by 5.38 points (95% CI 2.76 to 8.01; d = 0.60) and was stable across eight specifications. Four new self-report scales showed smaller differences (d = 0.12 to 0.29), none significant after Holm correction; each scale could detect only differences of about d = 0.4. The effect on expert ratings exceeded the mean effect on self-report by 0.37 standard deviations (95% CI 0.10 to 0.63). Component analyses were exploratory. The design cannot separate the contribution of AI from structured practice and feedback.

Rapid growth in biomedical literature has increased the need for auditable methods that convert article-level text into structured evidence data. Air pollution is increasingly framed as a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia, but publication growth alone does not indicate a structurally diverse evidence base. We aimed to develop and apply a human-validated large language model (LLM)-assisted role-analysis framework based on structured entity extraction to characterize recent air pollution–cognition evidence. Operationally, role-analysis retains pollutant and cognition-related entities as multi-label fields while assigning a single predominant study-level analytical role to each domain. We conducted an abstract-level evidence-structure analysis of PubMed-indexed human original studies published from 1 January 2020 through 22 March 2026. PubMed formed the primary analytic corpus, and Web of Science was used as a supplementary coverage check. A predefined coding schema was used to extract pollutants, cognitive outcomes, study designs, statistical methods, populations, data sources, geographic settings, and analytical roles from titles and abstracts. LLM-assisted screening, extraction, and role coding were constrained by field definitions, conservative coding rules, and consistency checks. Human validation evaluated screening, extraction, and role-coding outputs. Of the 1,061 PubMed records that entered the four-domain eligibility screening, 406 eligible studies were included. In the screening-validation sample ( n = 106), precision was 1.000, recall was 0.881, accuracy was 0.953, F1 score was 0.937, and Cohen’s κ was 0.899. In the structured-extraction and role-coding validation sample ( n = 81), field-level agreement ranged from 0.765 to 1.000; agreement was 0.926 for pollutant roles and 0.901 for cognition roles. The structured evidence dataset showed concentration around particulate matter and gaseous pollutants, older-adult populations, and cognitive outcomes including global cognitive performance, domain-specific cognition, and dementia-related outcomes. Direct pollutant exposure–cognitive outcome analyses dominated the role structure, whereas mediation, effect modification, and alternative role configurations were uncommon. Evidence sparsity reflected overlapping limitations in pollutant characterization, cognitive domain coverage, analytical role diversity, population representation, geographic distribution, and data-source dependence. The post-2020 air pollution–cognition literature is volume-rich but structurally uneven. A human-validated LLM-assisted role-analysis framework can convert biomedical abstracts into auditable evidence data that preserve multi-label study entities together with study-level analytical-role summaries and help distinguish growth in study volume from structural diversity of the evidence base.

documents.abstract: Nutrition science has traditionally focused on dietary intake, nutrient metabolism, physiology, and health outcomes. Although these domains remain fundamental, advancing public health increasingly requires understanding nutrition within the broader systems that shape food production, processing, access, consumption, and environmental sustainability. This Perspective proposes sustainable nutrition as a unifying concept: maintaining nutritional status that supports growth, development, and health across the lifespan while accounting for population needs, context, and the capacity and resilience of food systems. We describe a Nutritional Ecology framework that conceptualizes nutrition as the product of dynamic, reciprocal interactions among human biology, dietary patterns, food systems, and environmental conditions. Agricultural practices affect food quantity, quality, nutrient composition, biodiversity, water resources, greenhouse gas emissions, and ecosystem resilience, while environmental change influences crop productivity, nutrient density, food safety, and nutrition security. Dietary patterns simultaneously affect chronic disease risk and the environmental footprint of food systems. These interdependencies argue against evaluating human health and environmental sustainability in isolation. We therefore call for a transformation toward integrated, systems-based nutrition research that incorporates biological variability, environmental drivers, and system-level interactions. Multidisciplinary collaborations spanning nutrition, food, agricultural, environmental, epidemiologic, computational, systems, and implementation sciences will be essential. Emerging approaches, including systems mapping, network analysis, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and multiscale data integration, can identify trade-offs and leverage points for intervention. Integrating nutrition, food systems, and environmental science is a scientific necessity for generating evidence across diverse population contexts that supports resilient food systems, effective dietary guidance, improved clinical care, healthier people, and a healthier planet.

Assistive artificial intelligence systems for visually impaired users commonly address mobility and educational accessibility as separate computational tasks, resulting in fragmented architecture, redundant inference, and inefficient use of computational resources. This study presents SUSTAINABLESIGHT, a resource-aware vision–edge AI architecture intended for wearable deployment that integrates navigation perception and mathematical-expression recognition through shared, context-aware execution. The proposed architecture supports navigation (NAV), learning (LEARN), and hybrid (HYBRID) operating modes and employs a mode-aware scheduler to activate only the computational components required by the current task. A reproducible computational evaluation was conducted using public datasets and measured inference traces on a GPU runtime; no physical wearable device was evaluated. For navigation perception, YOLOv8n evaluated on the COCO 2017 validation set achieved a precision of 0.6343, recall of 0.4746, mAP@50 of 0.5188, and mAP@50–95 of 0.3681, with a mean inference latency of 7.24 ms on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU. Mathematical-expression recognition using pix2tex was evaluated on a fixed 500-expression subset of an Im2LaTeX validation dataset; 499 expressions were evaluable, with a mean normalized similarity of 0.5940, median similarity of 0.6394, and median character error rate of 0.4343. The substantially greater computational cost of mathematical recognition motivated adaptive branch activation. In a 1,000-request trace-driven workload, SUSTAINABLESIGHT maintained 100% request coverage while reducing model invocations from 2,000 to 1,098 (45.10%) and mean request latency from 3562.22 ms to 1311.32 ms (63.19%) relative to a fixed unified baseline. Mean-latency reductions of 16.15–81.61% were observed across five workload compositions, and scheduler ablation showed that avoiding unnecessary mathematical-recognition inference accounts for most of the latency improvement. Sustainability is assessed here as computational resource efficiency; device energy consumption and carbon emissions were not measured. These results indicate that SUSTAINABLESIGHT offers a reproducible, resource-aware basis for integrating mobility and STEM-accessibility workloads, while improved mathematical recognition, deployment of wearable edge hardware, and user validation remain important directions for future work.
