documents.abstract: Abstract Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

Abstract Background Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields. Objective In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field. Methods We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling. Results The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007‐0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=−46, and M3 Δ=−158 points). Scoring behavior analysis identified 2 intrinsically consistent but mutually inconsistent criterion-interpretation models. Rater 1’s scores were most consistent with the reasoning quality approach (partial credit to clinical competence independent of vignette context). Rater 2’s scores were most consistent with the context fidelity approach (near-zero scores for wrong vignette responses independent of reasoning quality). Contrary to the self-preference hypothesis, both raters placed the other higher-performing model above their own. Under rater 1, C6 (PARM reflection) was the lowest-scoring criterion across all 4 models, whereas rater 2 showed greater model-dependent variation in C6 scoring. Conclusions AI raters used in LLM-based clinical benchmarking do not behave as interchangeable scoring tools. Their scoring behavior is most consistent with model-specific criterion interpretation patterns that systematically produce different outcomes. The observed low interrater reliability requires interpretation rather than simply being ignored: it reflects structured, direction-specific disagreement concentrated in models with context-tracking failures, not random inconsistency. PARM reflection showed a notable yet evaluator-dependent scoring pattern that warranted further investigation, rather than being interpreted as an evaluator-independent deficit.

documents.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes may reduce documentation burden, but little is known about their adoption during enterprise-scale ambulatory rollout. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 2901 ambulatory clinicians at an integrated academic health system using linked electronic health record and vendor usage data from December 2024 through May 2025. Clinician adoption was defined as any use during the study period, and monthly visit-level uptake as the proportion of eligible ambulatory visits in which the ambient AI scribe was used. Adoption and uptake varied substantially across practice settings, specialties, and clinician types. Clinician-level adoption was highest in community internal medicine (67%), community general pediatrics (69%), and academic neurology (53%), and lowest in academic general surgery (16%), obstetrics and gynecology (18%), and psychiatry (19%). Community attending physicians and advanced practice providers showed marked increases in median visit-level uptake, reaching approximately 80%-90% in some groups by May 2025. Distinct longitudinal patterns included slow and steady adoption, early use followed by discontinuation, transient use, and late adoption. These findings suggest that implementation support and evaluation strategies should be tailored to local practice context rather than applied uniformly across a health system.

documents.abstract: Purpose This research aims to explore how generative AI (GenAI) recommendation modality (text vs voice) influences consumer recommendation adoption and how this effect further interacts with product type (search vs experience), processing fluency and multitasking to shape consumers’ behavioural responses to recommendations. Given that GenAI recommendation systems increasingly support interactive consumer decision-making, the authors examine modality as a key design feature shaping how GenAI-generated recommendations are delivered to consumers. Design/methodology/approach Across five studies, the authors examine how GenAI recommendation modality influences consumers’ recommendation adoption. The preliminary field study uses actual customer interactions in a natural commercial environment to establish the practical relevance of the phenomenon. Study 1 replicates the core modality effect in a controlled Chinese experiment. Study 2 examines the moderating role of product type. Studies 3 and 4 investigate processing fluency and multitasking as the underlying mechanism and boundary condition, using behavioural measures across all studies. Findings The findings demonstrate that GenAI recommendation modality affects consumers’ recommendation adoption, with text-based recommendations outperforming voice-based recommendations. The modality also interacts with product type and this effect is mediated by processing fluency: text-based recommendations elicit stronger behavioural responses for search products, whereas voice-based recommendations are more effective for experience products. Multitasking further moderates this pattern, favouring voice-based recommendations under high cognitive load across product types. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on controlled experimental settings and future work could examine additional contextual or individual-level moderators to enhance external validity. Practical implications Marketers should tailor GenAI recommendation modalities based on product type and anticipated multitasking environments. Text-based interactions are more suitable for detail-oriented search products, whereas voice-based interactions better suit experience products and multitasking contexts. Originality/value This research contributes to the GenAI literature by identifying recommendation modality as a critical yet understudied design feature of GenAI recommendation systems. The findings show that recommendation modality plays a central role in shaping consumer responses to GenAI-generated recommendations and extend processing fluency theory and task–technology fit by integrating product type and multitasking as key boundary conditions.
